title: Separate the meanings of Q
revised_question: Which structure is actually intended: Robinson arithmetic Q, a q-difference calculus, a p-adic field, or a formal power-series ring? What maps, if any, connect the chosen structures?
status: Definitions resolved with a structural obstruction
summary: The original notation can be repaired completely at the level of objects. Robinson arithmetic Q is a first-order theory, Q_p is a valued field of characteristic zero, F_p[[q]] is a formal power-series ring of characteristic p, and D_q is an operator depending on a numerical or formal parameter. A proposed connection must name the relevant category and map; the shared letter Q supplies neither.
definitions_json: ["Robinson Q consists of axioms in the language of zero, successor, addition and multiplication; it is not a number field.","Q_p is the completion of Q for |x|_p=p^(−v_p(x)); Z_p is its valuation ring.","F_p[[q]] consists of formal series Σa_n q^n. Its q-adic topology measures vanishing order, not numerical size.","D_q f(x)=(f(qx)−f(x))/((q−1)x), initially for q≠1 and x≠0."]
theorem_name: Characteristic obstructs a claimed field identification
theorem_statement: There is a canonical dense embedding Q→Q_p and a compatible reduction system Z_p→Z/p^nZ. There is no unital ring homomorphism Q_p→F_p[[q]], or in the reverse direction. In particular these objects cannot be identified by renaming their parameters.
theorem_proof: A unital homomorphism sends an integer n·1 to the same n·1. In characteristic p, p·1=0, whereas p is nonzero and invertible in Q_p. If φ:Q_p→F_p[[q]] were unital, then 1=φ(p p^(−1))=φ(p)φ(p^(−1))=0, a contradiction. In the reverse direction, applying φ to p·1=0 would give p·1=0 in Q_p, also impossible. The dense embedding Q→Q_p instead preserves characteristic and the field operations. The reductions from Z_p preserve ring operations but have nontrivial kernel p^nZ_p, so they are quotients rather than embeddings. This distinction already eliminates several possible informal identifications without requiring a difficult theorem.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare a rational number, a p-adic approximation and a formal series.","calculation":"The rational 1/3 maps into Q_7 and can be approximated by compatible residues modulo 7^n. The formal series (1−q)^(−1)=1+q+q²+⋯ belongs to F_7[[q]] because its coefficients satisfy a formal multiplication identity. Its formal variable q is not automatically the prime 7 or a neural-network parameter.","conclusion":"A corrected dictionary gives legitimate arrows and a proof that one tempting arrow cannot exist."}
limits: An arithmetic theory can be interpreted in structures, and equal-characteristic local fields can resemble mixed-characteristic fields in selected respects. The characteristic obstruction does not rule out every model-theoretic or categorical comparison; it rules out the specified unital ring identifications.
extension: For every later use of q or Q, record its type, admissible values and morphisms. A meaningful bridge should transport a named theorem, not merely an expression.

title: p-adic completion with certified digits
revised_question: How does completing Q in the p-adic norm change convergence and numerical precision, and which computations genuinely benefit?
status: Simple-root lifting proved and calculated
summary: A useful p-adic computation is a compatible sequence of exact congruences with a precision guarantee. The essential advantage in this example is that a simple solution modulo p determines one branch at every higher precision; decimal proximity has no role in the argument.
definitions_json: ["v_p(x) is the exponent of p in a nonzero rational x, and |0|_p=0.","An approximation x_n modulo p^n certifies a p-adic ball x_n+p^nZ_p.","A simple root modulo p satisfies f(x_1)≡0 and f′(x_1) not≡0 modulo p."]
theorem_name: Unique next digit in a Hensel lift
theorem_statement: For f∈Z_p[x], a simple root x_n modulo p^n has exactly one lift x_n+t p^n modulo p^(n+1), with t∈{0,…,p−1}. The compatible lifts converge to a unique root in x_1+pZ_p.
theorem_proof: Taylor expansion gives f(x_n+t p^n)≡f(x_n)+t p^n f′(x_n) modulo p^(n+1); all terms of degree at least two are divisible by p^(2n), hence by p^(n+1). Dividing by p^n reduces the lift equation to f(x_n)/p^n+t f′(x_n)≡0 modulo p. The derivative is a unit, so this linear equation has one digit t. Repeating constructs a compatible inverse-limit element. Completeness gives a limit α; polynomial continuity gives f(α)=0. If two roots share the residue x_1, the same unique-digit argument forces agreement modulo every p^n and therefore equality. A finite calculation consequently certifies a ball containing the unique branch, not an approximate real root.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Lift x²−2 from the root 3 modulo 7.","calculation":"At precision 7², write x=3+7t. Dividing f(x) by 7 gives 1+6t≡0 modulo 7, hence t=1 and x=10 modulo 49. Next x=10+49t gives 2+6t≡0, hence t=2 and x=108 modulo 343. Directly, 108²−2=34·343. The verifier continues the uniquely selected digits through precision 7^6.","conclusion":"The result is a root α∈Z_7 with α≡108 modulo 343, with a proof that no other root in 3+7Z_7 has those initial conditions."}
limits: If f′ vanishes modulo p, uniqueness and existence require a different argument; the simple-root calculation cannot be recycled unchanged. This example establishes an arithmetic algorithm, not a general computational speedup over real methods.
extension: Develop Newton lifting with precision doubling and an independent residual valuation; compare digit lifting and Newton lifting on the same branch.

title: Affine dynamics on Z_p
revised_question: For f(x)=ax+b on Z_p, which fixed points exist, when are they attracting, and what finite congruence data determines the orbit?
status: Complete fixed-point and attraction classification for the stated family
summary: The affine family can be settled exactly. The hypotheses a,b∈Z_p ensure that f(x)=ax+b maps Z_p into itself and never expands p-adic distance. Attracting, neutral and translational behavior can then be distinguished without metaphor.
definitions_json: ["A fixed point solves f(x*)=x*.","Attraction means f^n(x)→x* in the p-adic metric for nearby initial states.","Congruence modulo p^N means two states cannot be distinguished at N-digit precision."]
theorem_name: Affine fixed points and orbit differences
theorem_statement: If a≠1, a fixed point in Z_p exists exactly when b/(1−a)∈Z_p, equivalently b=0 or v_p(b)≥v_p(1−a), and is then unique. If a=1, b=0 makes every point fixed and b≠0 gives none. For |a|_p<1 the unique point attracts every state; for |a|_p=1 no distinct state converges to a fixed point.
theorem_proof: The fixed-point equation is (1−a)x=b, which gives the classification because Q_p is a field and membership in Z_p is exactly nonnegative valuation. Subtract two trajectories: f^n(x)−f^n(y)=a^n(x−y). Taking norms gives |a|_p^n|x−y|_p. This converges to zero precisely in the nonunit case, while for a unit it remains constant whenever x≠y. When |a|_p<1, 1−a is a unit, so every b supplies an integral fixed point. For a≠1, direct induction gives f^n(x)=a^n x+b(1−a^n)/(1−a). Congruent initial states remain congruent at every step, since multiplication by a∈Z_p cannot lower their agreement precision.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take p=7, a=7 and b=1.","calculation":"The fixed point is −1/6∈Z_7. Starting from x_0=0 gives x_n=1+7+⋯+7^(n−1), and x_n−x*=7^n/6. Its valuation is exactly n. Thus n iterations supply n correct base-seven digits. In contrast a=8,b=1 has no fixed point in Z_7 because (1−8)x=1 would require v_7(x)=−1.","conclusion":"The same affine notation yields global contraction in one case and a provable integral fixed-point obstruction in the other."}
limits: Neutral maps may have rich periodic structure modulo p^N; constant separation does not mean every orbit is constant. This classification is for affine maps on Z_p, not arbitrary nonlinear p-adic dynamics.
extension: Classify neutral affine cycles modulo p^N, then identify which cycle properties stabilize as N grows. Use gcd divisibility as an independent finite checker.

title: A valid probability model and identifiable parameters
revised_question: On what domain is the expression a probability, and can its parameters be identified from observations?
status: Range failure proved and a finite-design model specified
summary: The original product can be analyzed before any modeling claim is made. A formula is a probability only on an admissible domain, and fitted coefficients are meaningful only when the observation design can distinguish them.
definitions_json: ["For the original expression P(x,y)=(1+x)(1−y), assume x,y∈[0,1].","For the alternative logistic model let z=(1,x,y), η=z·β and σ(η)=1/(1+e^(−η)).","A finite design matrix X has rows z_i and identifies β when distinct coefficients give distinct modeled probability vectors."]
theorem_name: Exact admissible domain and logistic identifiability
theorem_statement: On [0,1]² the product lies in [0,1] exactly when y≥x/(1+x). A logistic model yields probabilities strictly between zero and one for every finite β. At a fixed design, its coefficient vector is identifiable exactly when X has full column rank.
theorem_proof: Nonnegativity of the product is automatic on the square. The upper bound is (1+x)(1−y)≤1, equivalent to y≥x/(1+x) because 1+x>0. The point (1,0) violates it with P=2. For the logistic family, σ is a strictly increasing bijection R→(0,1). Thus equal probability vectors are equivalent, after applying logit, to Xβ=Xβ′. Full column rank makes this imply β=β′; a nonzero null vector otherwise supplies indistinguishable coefficients. For independent Bernoulli observations the log likelihood is Σ[y_iη_i−log(1+e^η_i)]. Its Hessian is −XᵀWX with W diagonal and positive at finite β. Full rank gives strict concavity, but does not guarantee that a finite maximizer exists: complete separation can send the optimum to infinity.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Use the three design points (0,0),(1,0),(0,1).","calculation":"Their augmented rows form an invertible 3×3 matrix. β=(0,log3,−log3) gives probabilities (1/2,3/4,1/4). Taking logits yields (0,log3,−log3), from which β is uniquely recovered by solving the linear system. Repeating only the first point would identify β_0 but leave the other two coefficients free.","conclusion":"The example separates probability range, structural identifiability and existence of an estimator—three questions the original toy formula left unresolved."}
limits: Choosing a logistic family does not establish empirical truth, independence or adequate calibration. Identifiability is conditional on the design and model; it is not a performance guarantee.
extension: Add a specified observation model and investigate design conditioning or separation before optimizing the likelihood.

title: Specify a hard problem before using arithmetic complexity
revised_question: What exact computational problem is proposed, what is public, and what evidence or reduction supports its difficulty?
status: A toy encryption proposal is explicitly broken
summary: Sophisticated number systems do not themselves supply one-wayness. A mathematically assessable proposal must say what an adversary receives, what recovery problem is being claimed difficult, and how problem instances are distributed.
definitions_json: ["A toy modular scheme publishes a prime p and nonzero multiplier a and maps a message x to y=ax modulo p.","Correctness of a private recovery algorithm is different from hardness of public recovery.","An instance distribution specifies which public parameters, secrets and observations occur; worst-case difficulty alone need not control that distribution."]
theorem_name: Public linear arithmetic is publicly invertible
theorem_statement: For the stated toy map, every message is recovered from public data using x=a^(−1)y modulo p. Extended Euclid computes a^(−1), so adding large notation or expressing the same arithmetic p-adically cannot turn this construction into a secret inversion problem.
theorem_proof: Since p is prime and a is nonzero modulo p, gcd(a,p)=1. The extended Euclidean algorithm produces integers u,v with ua+vp=1. Reducing modulo p gives ua≡1, and multiplying y=ax by u recovers x≡uy. This is a deterministic polynomial-time attack in the bit length of p. More generally, a public invertible linear transformation over a field is inverted by linear algebra. If its matrix is hidden but an oracle permits arbitrary message queries, querying the coordinate basis recovers its columns. Neither attack needs to search the message space or exploit implementation defects. They attack the mathematical specification itself.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take p=101, a=7 and observed y=35.","calculation":"Euclid gives 7^(−1)≡29 modulo 101, since 7·29=203≡1. Therefore x≡29·35≡5. The verifier recovers x using only these public quantities. A larger prime changes the input size but not the kind of attack.","conclusion":"The construction is correct as a reversible encoding and fails as a claimed secret arithmetic trapdoor."}
limits: This example does not establish security or insecurity of an unrelated fully specified cryptosystem. A different map might pose a genuinely different problem, but its hardness must be argued independently of the prestige of its geometric or arithmetic vocabulary.
extension: For any proposed replacement, give generation, evaluation, recovery, correctness and an explicit public attack model. Test algebraic simplifications on small instances before attaching a security claim.

title: Zeno through a convergent series and a time law
revised_question: Which infinite sequence of distances has a finite sum, and what time parametrization permits the endpoint to be reached?
status: Convergence and endpoint behavior proved
summary: Infinitely many subdivisions do not determine elapsed time. Once both the distance increments and the time increments are stated, the mathematical ambiguity disappears: an infinite event sequence can accumulate at a finite time, or it can continue for an infinite duration.
definitions_json: ["Let distance increments be d_n=2^(−n), with milestones x_N=Σ_(n=1)^N d_n.","Let positive time increments be τ_n and milestone times t_N=Σ_(n=1)^N τ_n.","A finite accumulation time exists exactly when the positive time series converges."]
theorem_name: Finite distance does not fix finite elapsed time
theorem_statement: The distances sum to one. Choosing τ_n=2^(−n) reaches milestones at t_N=1−2^(−N) and admits the continuous extension x(1)=1. Choosing τ_n=1/n instead takes infinite total time while approaching the same spatial limit.
theorem_proof: For the geometric sum, multiply S_N=1/2+⋯+2^(−N) by two and subtract to obtain S_N=1−2^(−N). Given ε>0, choose N>log₂(1/ε); then 0<1−S_N<ε, proving convergence. With equal distance and time increments, the piecewise linear motion is simply x(t)=t on [0,1), so continuity supplies the endpoint x(1)=1. In the harmonic-time model, the subsequence of times diverges because each block from 2^k+1 through 2^(k+1) contributes at least 1/2. A continuous piecewise linear interpolation still approaches spatial position one, but only as t→∞. The number of labeled milestones is identical in both descriptions; its cardinality does not decide the total time.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare the first N milestones in the two parametrizations.","calculation":"Both have spatial coordinate 1−2^(−N). In the first model the remaining time is 2^(−N). In the second, any finite milestone leaves an infinite tail Σ_(n>N)1/n. Their different conclusions follow from different time assignments, not from a contradiction in summing the same distances.","conclusion":"The revised question separates convergence, continuity and parametrization, each of which can be proved with elementary estimates."}
limits: A mathematical parametrization does not assert that a physical device can execute an unbounded rate of discrete operations. The continuous trajectory requires no such discrete mechanism; a physical implementation would add its own constraints.
extension: Study rectifiable curves with infinitely many segments and ask separately whether a chosen parametrization has bounded speed, finite length and a continuous endpoint.

title: Octonions with a declared multiplication convention
revised_question: Which identities survive nonassociativity, and exactly when does regrouping an octonion product change its value?
status: Nonassociativity exhibited and Moufang law certified by all coefficients
summary: An analogy involving octonions becomes mathematics once multiplication, regrouping and the surviving identities are explicit. The real octonions are a division algebra but not an associative algebra; consequently their nonzero elements form a Moufang loop rather than a group.
definitions_json: ["Represent an octonion as a pair (a,b) of quaternions with product (a,b)(c,d)=(ac−conj(d)b, da+b conj(c)).","Use the quaternion convention ij=k, jk=i, ki=j. Set e1=(i,0), e2=(j,0), e3=(k,0), e4=(0,1), e5=(0,i), e6=(0,j), e7=(0,k).","The associator is [a,b,c]=(ab)c−a(bc). The Euclidean norm on R⁸ is multiplicative."]
theorem_name: A nonzero associator with an exact surviving identity
theorem_statement: Under this convention [e1,e2,e4]=2e7. Nevertheless the associator is alternating, and the Moufang identity (ab)(ca)=a((bc)a) holds for all real octonions. In particular any two elements generate an associative subalgebra, the classical alternative-algebra theorem.
theorem_proof: The displayed associator follows directly from e1e2=e3, e3e4=e7, e2e4=e6 and e1e6=−e7. For an independent finite certificate of alternation, expand the trilinear associator in the basis 1,e1,…,e7. The verifier checks all 512 triples and confirms [a,b,c]+[b,a,c]=0 and [a,b,c]+[a,c,b]=0 at every coefficient. Bilinearity of multiplication then proves alternation for arbitrary real coordinates. The Moufang residual is quadratic in a and linear in b and c. It is therefore enough to check a on each basis vector and each pairwise sum of basis vectors, with b and c on basis vectors: polarization recovers all squared and mixed coefficients. All 2304 evaluations vanish exactly. This finite coefficient certificate verifies the full identity, not merely a random sample.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Regroup e1,e2,e4 and compare the two results.","calculation":"The left grouping gives (e1e2)e4=e7 and the right gives e1(e2e4)=−e7. Their difference has norm two. If the third factor instead belongs to the associative quaternion algebra generated by e1,e2, regrouping makes no difference.","conclusion":"The example demonstrates both a genuine failure and a precise replacement law. No philosophical interpretation is needed for either statement."}
limits: Other octonion tables may change basis signs and the displayed associator sign. The convention must travel with every numerical example. Alternativity does not authorize arbitrary reassociation of three unrelated factors.
extension: Use the explicit coefficient tensor as an exact algebraic input when investigating invariant subalgebras, automorphisms or defect loci.

title: The sharp octonion regrouping bound
revised_question: Can a regrouping defect be bounded quantitatively, and which invariances must such a bound respect?
status: Sharp inequality proved with an equality example
summary: The earlier proposal to measure a regrouping defect can be carried to a sharp result. The defect is not just a qualitative marker: its exact universal scale follows from norm multiplicativity, and a basis triple attains that scale.
definitions_json: ["For octonions define d(a,b,c)=||(ab)c−a(bc)||.","Let n=||a||||b||||c||. Norm multiplicativity gives ||(ab)c||=||a(bc)||=n.","For unit factors the squared defect is 2−2⟨(ab)c,a(bc)⟩, using the Euclidean inner product."]
theorem_name: Sharp norm bound and equality criterion
theorem_statement: For all real octonions, 0≤d(a,b,c)≤2||a||||b||||c||. If n>0, equality holds exactly when (ab)c=−a(bc). The constant two is optimal.
theorem_proof: Write u=(ab)c and v=a(bc). The triangle inequality gives ||u−v||≤||u||+||v||=2n. Alternatively, expand the squared norm: ||u−v||²=2n²−2⟨u,v⟩. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ⟨u,v⟩≥−n². Equality requires u and v to be oppositely directed; because their norms are equal and nonzero, this is exactly u=−v. The declared convention in M007 gives u=e7 and v=−e7 for a=e1,b=e2,c=e4, so the bound is attained at unit norm. Trilinearity also gives d(ra,sb,tc)=|rst|d(a,b,c) for real scalars. A norm-preserving algebra automorphism transports the associator and therefore preserves the defect.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Evaluate the normalized defect on a maximally nonassociative basis triple and an associative quaternion triple.","calculation":"For (e1,e2,e4), d=2. For (e1,e2,e3), both products equal −1, so d=0. The two calculations sit at opposite endpoints of the proved interval. The normalized quantity δ=d/(||a||||b||||c||) is consequently dimensionless on nonzero triples and ranges through values in [0,2].","conclusion":"The revised concept now has a universal bound, a certified sharpness witness, scale behavior and an exact criterion for attaining the upper endpoint."}
limits: This does not classify every zero-defect triple or every orbit of the automorphism group. A zero associator for one triple alone should not be promoted to a statement that an entire generated algebra is associative.
extension: Study the polynomial zero locus [a,b,c]=0 on three unit spheres and its orbit structure. Distinguish this classification problem from the sharp inequality already proved.

title: Hyperbolic identities that actually verify a wave
revised_question: Which derivative and algebraic identities are actually needed to verify a sech² travelling wave?
status: Exact derivative and travelling-wave calculation
summary: The corrected sech² identity supplies enough structure to verify a whole travelling-wave family. Instead of recognizing a familiar shape, we derive the amplitude-speed relation required by a specified nonlinear PDE.
definitions_json: ["Let T=tanh z and f(z)=sech²z=1−T².","The derivatives satisfy T′=f, f′=−2fT and d/dz=(1−T²)d/dT when applied to polynomials in T.","For a wave u(x,t)=A f(κ(x−ct−x0)), primes on u below denote spatial derivatives."]
theorem_name: Amplitude and velocity are fixed by substitution
theorem_statement: For nonzero κ and the equation u_t+6uu_x+u_xxx=0, the sech² ansatz is a solution when A=2κ² and c=4κ². These constants are linked by the equation; they cannot be chosen independently.
theorem_proof: Differentiate f′=−2fT to obtain f″=−2f′T−2fT′=4fT²−2f²=4f−6f². Differentiating again gives f‴=(4−12f)f′. After rescaling, u_xxx=4κ²u_x−(12κ²/A)u u_x. The travelling-wave time derivative is u_t=−c u_x. The PDE residual is therefore (4κ²−c)u_x+(6−12κ²/A)u u_x. The stated amplitude and speed annihilate both coefficients. Conversely, for a nonconstant profile with A≠0, vanishing for the whole wave forces those coefficients to vanish because u takes a nontrivial interval of values wherever u_x is nonzero. The verifier independently represents u=2(1−T²) as a polynomial and obtains an identically zero residual using exact integer coefficients.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Use κ=1, x0=0.","calculation":"Then u=2sech²(x−4t). Its maximum is two at x=4t and its spatial integral is four, since ∫sech²z dz=tanh z. The profile is localized and translates with speed four. A version with amplitude six and the same width would not solve this normalization of KdV.","conclusion":"The identity repair now produces a complete exact check, conserved profile mass and a falsifiable relationship among width, height and speed."}
limits: Changing the sign or coefficient of the nonlinear term changes the amplitude relation. This calculation verifies an explicit family and is not a classification of all solutions or a stability proof.
extension: Use the first integrals of the travelling-wave ODE to classify decaying profiles under explicit smoothness and boundary assumptions.

title: Gudermannian coordinates with the measure retained
revised_question: What does the Gudermannian simplify, and what Jacobian and endpoint singularities does the simplification introduce?
status: An exact coordinate transformation and endpoint asymptotic
summary: The Gudermannian is a genuine bridge between hyperbolic and circular expressions. Its advantage is algebraic simplification on a bounded angular interval; its cost is a singular inverse-coordinate derivative near that interval’s endpoints.
definitions_json: ["Set θ=gd(x)=arctan(sinh x), mapping R bijectively to (−π/2,π/2).","Then sinθ=tanh x, cosθ=sech x and θ′=cosθ.","The inverse is x=asinh(tanθ)=artanh(sinθ), with dx/dθ=secθ."]
theorem_name: Transforming derivatives and integrals consistently
theorem_statement: For a smooth function F(θ), ∂_xF=cosθ F_θ and ∂_x²F=cos²θ F_θθ−sinθ cosθ F_θ. For an integrable profile u(x)=U(gd(x)), ∫_R u(x)dx=∫_(−π/2)^(π/2)U(θ)secθ dθ. The angular compression does not discard this Jacobian.
theorem_proof: Differentiate θ=arctan(sinh x): θ′=cosh x/(1+sinh²x)=sech x. Its range and monotonicity show it is a bijection. Since cosθ is positive in that range, the elementary identities follow by resolving a right triangle with tangent sinh x. The differential operator is ∂_x=cosθ∂_θ; applying it twice gives the stated second derivative. The ordinary change-of-variables theorem supplies dx=secθdθ. For x→+∞, π/2−gd(x)=2arctan(e^(−x))∼2e^(−x). Hence the inverse sensitivity secθ grows like 1/(π/2−θ). Bounded angular coordinates therefore do not guarantee bounded recovery error in x.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Transform u(x)=Asech²x.","calculation":"The angular profile is U(θ)=Acos²θ. Retaining the measure gives ∫u dx=A∫cosθdθ=2A, matching the direct calculation A[tanh x]_(−∞)^∞. If one integrated Acos²θ against dθ without the Jacobian, the answer would instead be Aπ/2 and would describe a different measure.","conclusion":"The transformation simplifies a profile while preserving its integral only when the derivative and measure factors are carried along."}
limits: For a moving coordinate θ=gd(κ(x−ct)), time differentiation also contributes θ_t=−cκcosθ. A stationary spatial formula cannot simply be inserted into a time-dependent PDE without this extra chain rule.
extension: Transform an entire variational problem or PDE, including boundary conditions, noise and observation measure; assess conditioning in the transformed metric.

title: KdV and KP with matched conventions
revised_question: Which PDE and normalization are we solving, and how does a one-dimensional soliton embed into KP?
status: One-dimensional family and oblique KP line wave verified
summary: KdV is an evolution equation in one spatial coordinate. KP adds a second spatial coordinate and a sign that changes its transverse behavior. An exact KdV solution embeds in either stated KP sign when it is independent of the second coordinate, but this elementary inclusion does not solve the full two-dimensional problem.
definitions_json: ["Fix KdV as u_t+6uu_x+u_xxx=0.","Fix KP as (u_t+6uu_x+u_xxx)_x+3σu_yy=0 with σ=±1.","A line-wave phase is η=kx+ly−ωt+δ with real k≠0 and l,δ; set U(η)=(k²/2)sech²(η/2)."]
theorem_name: An explicit KP line-wave dispersion relation
theorem_statement: The profile u(x,y,t)=U(kx+ly−ωt+δ) solves the stated KP equation when ω=k³+3σl²/k. Taking l=0 recovers the KdV family of M009 after k=2κ.
theorem_proof: The travelling-wave derivative identity in the phase variable is U‴=U′−(6/k²)UU′. Thus the expression inside the outer x derivative is −ωU′+6kUU′+k³U‴=(k³−ω)U′. Its x derivative is k(k³−ω)U″, while u_yy=l²U″. The KP residual is [k(k³−ω)+3σl²]U″ and vanishes under the displayed relation. With l=0, η=2κ(x−4κ²t−x0), giving precisely 2κ²sech²(κ(x−4κ²t−x0)). This calculation fixes every coefficient and sign directly rather than inferring them from a remembered formula.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Choose σ=+1, k=2, l=1 and δ=0.","calculation":"Then ω=8+3/2=19/2, and u=2sech²((2x+y−(19/2)t)/2). The crest is the straight line 2x+y=(19/2)t. It is localized in the normal direction but extends along the line, so its total integral over the whole plane is not finite.","conclusion":"The line wave is an exactly verified two-dimensional solution with a clear localization limitation."}
limits: Neither transverse stability nor general KP multi-soliton classification follows from this substitution. The signs σ=±1 must remain explicit, and conventions in external references may use time or field rescalings.
extension: Introduce a tau-function compatible with the same convention and study a genuine interaction of nonparallel line solitons rather than adding individual profiles.
references_json: [{"label":"Biondini and Chakravarty Soliton solutions of the KP II equation","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/nlin/0511068"}]

title: A complete two-soliton construction in a fixed KdV convention
revised_question: What interaction terms must a two-soliton solution contain, and when is the resulting tau-function nonsingular?
status: Tau-function interaction and phase shifts derived
summary: The interaction term can be determined rather than guessed. A positive tau-function supplies a nonsingular exact solution and gives a clean explanation of why the answer is not the sum of two single waves.
definitions_json: ["Take k1>k2>0, η_i=k_i x−k_i³t+δ_i and A=((k1−k2)/(k1+k2))².","Set τ=1+e^η1+e^η2+A e^(η1+η2), and u=2∂_x²logτ.","For exponentials, a Hirota bilinear operator acts by parameter differences; write P(k,ω)=kω+k⁴."]
theorem_name: Interaction coefficient and asymptotic shifts
theorem_statement: This τ obeys (D_xD_t+D_x⁴)τ·τ=0 and u solves u_t+6uu_x+u_xxx=0. The fast wave’s spatial shift is −log(A)/k1>0 and the slow wave’s is log(A)/k2<0. The profile mass is 2(k1+k2).
theorem_proof: Each one-wave term satisfies P(k_i,−k_i³)=0. The only new mixed exponential coefficient is proportional to A P(k1+k2,−k1³−k2³)+P(k1−k2,−k1³+k2³). These two polynomial values are 3k1k2(k1+k2)² and −3k1k2(k1−k2)², so their cancellation forces the stated A. Other coefficients reduce to the one-wave dispersion equations. Dividing the bilinear identity by τ² gives (logτ)_xt+(logτ)_xxxx+6((logτ)_xx)²=0; differentiating in x yields KdV for u. Because all four tau coefficients are positive, τ>0 for real x,t, eliminating zeros and singularities. In the fast moving frame, the effective one-wave factor changes from 1+e^η1 to 1+A e^η1 between early and late times, giving the fast shift. In the slow frame the factor changes in the reverse order, giving the slow shift. Finally ∫u dx=2[(logτ)_x]_(−∞)^∞=2(k1+k2).

Direct rational differentiation gives u(0,0)=153/98≈1.56122, whereas adding the two isolated wave values gives 5/2. The verifier checks every bilinear exponential coefficient exactly at three distinct rational parameter pairs; the preceding symbolic coefficient calculation proves the full parameter family.","conclusion":"The interaction coefficient, nonsingularity, mass and phase shifts are all specified and derived within one consistent normalization."}

title: Radial conservation and stereographic geometry
revised_question: Which power law follows from conserved radial flux, and which metric factor follows from a coordinate projection?
status: Two distinct inverse-power mechanisms calculated
summary: A coordinate projection and a conserved flux are mathematically different constructions. Each can generate a position-dependent factor, but the factors belong to different measures and have different meanings. Writing both down makes the proposed identification testable.
definitions_json: ["In Euclidean R^d with d≥2, a radial field has the form J(x)=F(r)e_r for r=||x||>0.","Conserved outward flux across a sphere means F(r) times its area is independent of r.","Stereographic coordinates (u,v) on the unit sphere use r²=u²+v² and X=(2u,2v,r²−1)/(1+r²)."]
theorem_name: Flux power law versus a projection Jacobian
theorem_statement: A rotationally symmetric conserved flux in dimension d has F(r)=C/r^(d−1), giving inverse-square magnitude in d=3. The unit-sphere stereographic metric is ds²=4(du²+dv²)/(1+u²+v²)² and its area measure is 4du dv/(1+u²+v²)². The latter is not a derivation of the former.
theorem_proof: The sphere of radius r has area ω_(d−1)r^(d−1). If its flux is Φ, then Φ=ω_(d−1)r^(d−1)F(r), yielding F(r)=Φ/(ω_(d−1)r^(d−1)). Equivalently, away from a source, the radial divergence is r^(1−d)∂_r(r^(d−1)F), which must vanish. For the projection, differentiate the displayed map X(u,v), take Euclidean inner products of its two coordinate derivatives and obtain a diagonal pullback metric with both diagonal entries 4/(1+r²)². Taking the square root of the determinant supplies the stated area factor. This second calculation concerns how one surface is charted, not how a physical flux changes across a family of spheres.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare the large-distance factors in their own variables.","calculation":"A three-dimensional radial flux decays as physical radius R^(−2). The stereographic area density decays as chart radius r^(−4). These statements do not contradict each other: R labels different spheres in a physical space, whereas r labels positions within a chart of one unit sphere. Identifying them would discard the very geometric distinction being calculated.","conclusion":"The original question now has a derivation of each factor and a concrete reason the coordinate formula does not imply the conservation law."}
limits: A projected representation of a conserved field can of course be constructed. It must transform the field and the integration measure together; conservation is then transported, not created by projection.
extension: Pull back a specified flux form into stereographic coordinates and verify the invariant integral explicitly, including the missing chart point.

title: q-differentiation of the Gudermannian
revised_question: Is there a specific q-difference identity involving gd, or are these two independently chosen tools?
status: An exact secant integral and uniform bounds
summary: There is a clean identity connecting q-differentiation and gd, but it is an instance of the fundamental theorem of calculus rather than evidence of a special learning mechanism. It allows the q-difference quotient to be bounded and its ordinary-derivative limit to be controlled.
definitions_json: ["For real q>0, q≠1 and x≠0, define D_qf(x)=(f(qx)−f(x))/((q−1)x).","Define D_qgd(0)=1 by continuous extension.","Let m=min(1,q) and M=max(1,q). On the interval between x and qx, the absolute coordinate lies between m|x| and M|x|."]
theorem_name: Exact integral representation and bounds
theorem_statement: D_qgd(x)=∫_0^1 sech(x(1+s(q−1)))ds. Consequently sech(M|x|)≤D_qgd(x)≤sech(m|x|). As q→1 these quotients converge to sech x uniformly on compact x-intervals.
theorem_proof: Since gd′(t)=sech t, subtracting its values gives gd(qx)−gd(x)=∫_x^(qx)sech t dt. Substitute t=x+s(q−1)x; the oriented integral and denominator cancel even when q<1 or x<0, proving the formula. The function sech t is positive, even and decreasing as |t| increases, so its extrema on this same-sign interval give the bounds. For x in a compact interval and q in a sufficiently small neighborhood of one, all arguments remain in a common compact interval. Uniform continuity of sech there makes the integrand converge uniformly, hence the averaged quotients converge uniformly. At x=0 the integrand equals one, proving the claimed extension without division by zero.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare q=1/2 and q=2 at x=2.","calculation":"The first quotient averages sech between 1 and 2; the second averages it between 2 and 4. Both are positive, and the verifier checks their values against the exact endpoint bounds. These are secant averages over different intervals, not two names for the same local derivative.","conclusion":"The relation is exact and has a precise limit. It distinguishes an honest q-difference calculation from a purely verbal association."}
limits: Replacing an ordinary gradient by D_q changes the optimization method and its chain rule. For products, D_q(fg)=g(x)D_qf+f(qx)D_qg; the ordinary Leibniz formula is recovered only in the limit. No improved learning performance follows from positivity or the bounds alone.
extension: Analyze a specified q-gradient iteration, derive its actual descent conditions and compare it with ordinary gradient descent under matched evaluation costs.

title: Quantitative Jacobian bounds for deep compositions
revised_question: Can a proposed layer construction bound products of Jacobians better than a conventional layer, and under which input distribution?
status: Vanishing demonstrated and a residual-depth bound derived
summary: A bounded activation does not protect its derivative from saturation. For gd the derivative is explicitly sech, so useful depth bounds can be derived without guessing from wave-propagation analogies. A residual scaling offers a separate, conditional way to control conditioning as depth grows.
definitions_json: ["For scalar layers h_l=gd(w_l h_(l−1)+b_l), write z_l=w_l h_(l−1)+b_l.","The input derivative is J=∏_(l=1)^L w_l sech z_l.","For vector layers the Jacobian is D_lW_l with D_l diagonal and entries sech of the preactivations. For the residual construction take T>0 and K≥0. Singular-value bounds must use all relevant coordinates."]
theorem_name: Saturation bound and a depth-scaled residual alternative
theorem_statement: If |w_l|≤W and every scalar |z_l|≥a>0, then |J|≤(W sech a)^L. For residual maps x_(l+1)=x_l+(T/L)F_l(x_l) with ||DF_l||₂≤K and L>TK, every total-Jacobian singular value lies between (1−TK/L)^L and (1+TK/L)^L. For L≥2TK, the bounds e^(−2TK) and e^(TK) are uniform in depth.
theorem_proof: The scalar chain rule gives the product, and monotonicity of sech on nonnegative arguments supplies the first estimate. In a residual layer, write its Jacobian I+E with ||E||≤TK/L. For every vector v, the triangle and reverse triangle inequalities give (1−||E||)||v||≤||(I+E)v||≤(1+||E||)||v||. Multiply the singular-value bounds across layers. The upper uniform estimate follows from log(1+s)≤s. For s≤1/2, log(1−s)≥−2s gives the lower estimate. These are worst-case deterministic bounds, conditional on a common derivative bound K; they make no distributional or performance claim.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Use h_(l+1)=gd(h_l+2), h_0=0, with L=20.","calculation":"Every preactivation is at least two. Therefore |J|≤sech(2)^20≈3.09865×10^(−12). Direct accumulation of logarithmic derivatives gives approximately 1.82740×10^(−24), far smaller still. The calculation avoids underflow and illustrates that the proved upper bound need not be sharp for a particular trajectory.","conclusion":"The original concern is now expressed as a measurable derivative contraction, alongside a different architecture with an explicit conditional depth guarantee."}
limits: The residual lower bound does not imply successful training, identifiability or useful representations. The gd upper bound for a vector layer requires control of the operator norm of its whole diagonal derivative matrix, not merely one saturated coordinate.
extension: Test whether a proposed layer family maintains the required K and singular-value conditions on its actual state domain; compare those certificates with measured gradients.

title: Minimal universal recurrences on an observable quotient
revised_question: Which sequence of observables satisfies a finite recurrence, and can the minimal polynomial give a shorter recurrence than the characteristic polynomial?
status: An exact annihilator theorem with a reduced example
summary: Cayley–Hamilton always gives a recurrence for a finite linear state, but the observable behavior may require a strictly smaller polynomial. The correct object is the induced operator after all permanently invisible directions have been quotiented out.
definitions_json: ["Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field, A:V→V and C:V→Y linear, with outputs y_n=CA^n x.","Let N=∩_(k=0)^(n−1)ker(CA^k), where n=dimV. Cayley–Hamilton makes this the intersection over all k≥0.","A universal output recurrence with polynomial p means CA^k p(A)x=0 for every state x and every k≥0."]
theorem_name: The observable quotient’s minimal polynomial is the universal recurrence
theorem_statement: N is A-invariant, so A induces A_bar on V/N. A polynomial p gives a universal output recurrence exactly when p(A_bar)=0. Thus the unique least-degree monic universal recurrence is the minimal polynomial of A_bar. Its degree is at most dim(V/N); for a scalar observable with an observable quotient it equals that quotient dimension.
theorem_proof: If v∈N, all outputs CA^kv vanish, hence CA^k(Av)=CA^(k+1)v=0 and Av∈N. Now a recurrence holds exactly when p(A)V⊂N, which is precisely p(A_bar)=0 after applying the quotient map. This proves both directions and minimality. The dimension bound is the standard minimal-polynomial bound. For scalar output, the row span of C,CA,… on the quotient has full dimension by observability. A polynomial of smaller degree would make every later row a combination of fewer initial rows, contradicting full dimension. This last equality need not hold for multiple outputs: A=I with C=I observes an n-dimensional state but has universal polynomial z−1.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take A=diag(1,2,3) and C=(1,1,0).","calculation":"The invisible space is span(e3). On the two-dimensional quotient the minimal polynomial is (z−1)(z−2), so y_(n+2)−3y_(n+1)+2y_n=0 for every initial state. The full characteristic polynomial has a redundant factor z−3. If the particular initial state is e1, its individual sequence satisfies the shorter recurrence y_(n+1)=y_n.","conclusion":"This distinguishes full-state, universal-observation and single-trajectory recurrences, rather than conflating their orders."}
limits: A recurrence fitted to one finite prefix may be accidental. The quotient argument proves a recurrence for all times under the stated model; finite fitting alone does not.
extension: Compute exact observability kernels and Hankel ranks, then certify the smallest realization compatible with the desired class of initial conditions.

title: The reachable and observable parts of a realization
revised_question: Which states can inputs reach, which states outputs distinguish, and what is the smallest realization preserving the input-output map?
status: Minimal zero-initial-state quotient constructed
summary: Reachability and observability answer different questions. Their intersection structure determines which internal modes affect driven input-output behavior from zero initial state. A mode can be unstable and entirely absent from the transfer function, making the initial-condition convention essential.
definitions_json: ["For a finite-dimensional real or complex system ẋ=Ax+Bu and y=Cx+Du with locally integrable inputs, define R=span{A^k imB:k≥0}, the reachable subspace.","Let N=∩_(k≥0)ker(CA^k), the unobservable subspace.","Both R and N are A-invariant, and the transfer function is H(s)=C(sI−A)^(−1)B+D where the resolvent exists."]
theorem_name: The zero-initial input-output state lives on R/(R∩N)
theorem_statement: Restriction to R discards modes no input can excite from zero. Quotienting by R∩N then discards modes no output can detect. The resulting realization is reachable and observable and has the same zero-initial input-output map; its dimension is the standard minimal realization order.
theorem_proof: Starting at zero, the variation-of-constants formula x(t)=∫_0^t e^(A(t−s))Bu(s)ds lies in R because that subspace is A-invariant and contains imB. Adding a state in R∩N never changes any subsequent output, including under common future inputs, so the quotient preserves the response. Conversely, all reachable quotient states are generated by the projected input, and an invisible quotient class would have a representative in N, hence in R∩N, so it is zero. These properties characterize the usual minimal finite-dimensional realization. Replacing the zero initial condition by arbitrary initial states changes the target: visible but unreachable modes can now contribute.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take A=diag(−1,−2,3), B=(1,0,1)^T and C=(1,1,0).","calculation":"R=span(e1,e3), while N=span(e3). The minimal driven state therefore has dimension one and transfer function 1/(s+1). The internally unstable e3 mode is reachable but invisible. The e2 mode is visible but unreachable; it matters for initial condition e2, producing e^(−2t), but not for zero-initial driven responses.","conclusion":"The example has reachable rank two and observable rank two, yet minimal driven order one. Merely taking either rank misses the intersection."}
limits: A stable transfer function does not establish internal stability when an unstable canceled mode remains. No empirical sensor claim follows without a correct state and observation model.
extension: Use exact basis changes to expose the four Kalman blocks and compare driven, arbitrary-initial-state and noisy-observation specifications.

title: Exact finite closure and a polynomial obstruction
revised_question: Does the PDE preserve a finite-dimensional invariant space on which a matrix identity can legitimately be used?
status: Invariant heat subspace and nonlinear no-go result proved
summary: A finite matrix can represent an infinite-dimensional evolution exactly on a proved invariant subspace. A truncation outside such a subspace instead produces an approximation. The distinction can be settled in examples, and a useful degree argument rules out a broad polynomial closure proposal.
definitions_json: ["A subspace W of observables is Koopman-invariant for a map f when p∈W implies p∘f∈W.","For the periodic heat equation u_t=u_xx, trigonometric modes are eigenfunctions of the generator ∂_xx.","For the obstruction, work with real polynomials as functions on an interval, and let f have degree d≥2."]
theorem_name: No finite polynomial Koopman space can contain the state coordinate
theorem_statement: There is no finite-dimensional subspace W⊂R[x] that contains x and is invariant under p↦p∘f when degf=d≥2. In contrast, the heat equation exactly preserves every fixed finite span of Fourier modes.
theorem_proof: If W contains x and is invariant, it contains x∘f=f, then f∘f, and inductively every iterate f^(∘n). Their degrees are d^n because the nonzero leading coefficient of a composition cannot cancel. Polynomials with distinct degrees are linearly independent: in any finite linear combination the largest degree has a coefficient contributed by exactly one summand, so that coefficient must vanish, and descending induction eliminates the rest. Thus W would contain infinitely many independent vectors, a contradiction. For heat flow, ∂_xx sin(kx)=−k²sin(kx) and the same holds for cos(kx), while the constant mode has eigenvalue zero. This proves invariance of each chosen finite mode span and gives exact coefficient evolution a_k(t)=e^(−k²t)a_k(0).
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare the logistic map and a nonlinear PDE stencil.","calculation":"For f(x)=2x(1−x), exact iterates have degrees 1,2,4,8,16,32,64 starting with x. No finite polynomial feature list containing x closes exactly on an interval. For Burgers-type nonlinearity u u_x, the initial mode sinx immediately generates sinx cosx=(1/2)sin2x, so the single-mode span is not invariant even though it is invariant for heat flow.","conclusion":"Finite polynomial degree growth gives a proof of impossibility, while Fourier invariance gives a valid exact finite example. Neither conclusion rests on a numerical residual alone."}
limits: The obstruction does not exclude nonpolynomial coordinate transformations, finite-state restrictions, approximate closures or special higher-dimensional nonlinear systems. On a finite orbit, polynomials are functions modulo additional relations and the interval argument no longer applies.
extension: Before applying Cayley–Hamilton to a nonlinear model, certify an invariant feature space or quantify the projection error. Investigate special model classes separately rather than assuming universal finite closure.
references_json: [{"label":"Brunton and coauthors Koopman invariant subspaces and finite linear representations","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.03007"},{"label":"Finite dimensional Koopman form of polynomial nonlinear systems","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.06557"}]

title: Hardy–BMO duality from atoms
revised_question: Which Hardy space is meant, and what bounded pairing does BMO provide on that space?
status: Classical estimate proved; duality theorem identified
summary: The useful connection is a bounded pairing between a cancellation-sensitive signal space and a mean-oscillation space. This supplies an actual inequality; it does not make arbitrary behavior into a Hardy-space object.
definitions_json: ["A real H¹ atom a is supported in a finite interval I, satisfies ∫a=0 and ||a||∞≤1/|I|. Higher dimensions use cubes or balls.","The BMO seminorm is sup_I |I|⁻¹∫_I|b−b_I|, where b_I is the interval average. Constants have seminorm zero.","The atomic H¹ norm is the infimum of Σ|λ_j| over convergent atomic decompositions f=Σλ_j a_j. This is not the Sobolev H¹ norm."]
theorem_name: Cancellation converts mean oscillation into a bounded functional
theorem_statement: For an atom a and b∈BMO, |∫ab|≤||b||_BMO. Consequently |⟨f,b⟩|≤||f||_H¹,atomic ||b||_BMO. The converse identification of every bounded H¹ functional with BMO modulo constants is the classical duality theorem, not a conclusion of the finite example alone.
theorem_proof: Subtract the constant b_I inside the pairing: ∫ab=∫_I a(b−b_I), because ∫a=0. The atom bound gives |∫ab|≤|I|⁻¹∫_I|b−b_I|≤||b||_BMO. For a finite atomic sum, apply the triangle inequality and sum the coefficient magnitudes. Completion gives the bounded functional on the atomic space. The quotient by constants is forced by cancellation: adding c to b leaves every atom pairing unchanged. The difficult converse is a representation theorem and requires the established Hardy-space theory; no finite rank calculation can replace it.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take I=[−1,1], a(x)=−1/2 on (−1,0), a(x)=1/2 on (0,1), and zero outside. Let b(x)=sign(x).","calculation":"The atom has zero integral and supremum 1/2. For any interval containing positive fraction t and negative fraction 1−t, the mean oscillation of sign is 4t(1−t)≤1. Symmetric intervals achieve 1. The pairing is ∫ab=1, so the atomic estimate is sharp for this normalization.","conclusion":"A normalization, a cancellation condition and a sharp example replace the earlier loose invocation of two named function spaces."}
limits: Pairings of general distributions require the continuous extension, not an unjustified pointwise integral. Graph analogues need their own measure, Laplacian and atomic definitions; the Euclidean theorem is not automatically inherited.
extension: Define graph atoms with respect to an explicit reversible measure, then ask whether the chosen graph-BMO space is the dual of the chosen graph Hardy space. Proving just the atom bound is a useful first stage, but it is not full duality.

title: A complete heat-signature collision
revised_question: Which objects can a chosen heat signature distinguish, and how stable is it to perturbations and sampling?
status: Classical pair with exact finite certificate
summary: The 4×4 rook graph and the Shrikhande graph supply an exact obstruction to recovering a graph from its heat trace or diagonal heat signature. The full heat operator retains strictly more information.
definitions_json: ["Both graphs have vertex set Z₄×Z₄. Rook adjacency means sharing exactly one coordinate.","Shrikhande adjacency means the difference lies in {(±1,0),(0,±1),(1,1),(−1,−1)} modulo four.","For adjacency A, L=6I−A and K_t=exp(−tL). The heat trace is Tr K_t; the vertex signature is (K_t)_{vv}."]
theorem_name: Identical spectra and vertex signatures do not force isomorphism
theorem_statement: Both graphs have Laplacian eigenvalues 0 once, 4 six times and 8 nine times, and every vertex in both has signature (1+6e^(−4t)+9e^(−8t))/16. Nevertheless their clique numbers are respectively four and three.
theorem_proof: The verifier constructs both integer adjacency matrices and checks A²=4I+2J. The all-ones vector has adjacency eigenvalue six. On its orthogonal complement J vanishes, so adjacency eigenvalues are ±2. Trace A=0 and dimension sixteen force multiplicities six and nine. Both graphs are connected because their Cayley generators span Z₄², hence eigenvalue six is simple. Their vertex translations act transitively, so all diagonal entries of any matrix function of A agree and equal its trace divided by sixteen. The verifier exhaustively checks four-vertex subsets: rook four-cliques exist, whereas Shrikhande has none, and Shrikhande has triangles. Clique number is invariant under isomorphism, proving the graphs differ.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Use the two explicit sixteen-vertex adjacency matrices produced by rook_adjacency() and shrikhande_adjacency() in verify.py.","calculation":"Exact matrix multiplication verifies the common-neighbor identity. Exhaustive enumeration of C(16,4)=1820 subsets per graph certifies the four-clique distinction. This does not rely on floating eigenvalue comparisons or a graph-isomorphism heuristic.","conclusion":"Even the entire curve of diagonal heat signatures can lose structural information. This is a stronger failure than matching a handful of sampled times."}
limits: The obstruction does not apply to the complete labeled K_t. For any fixed t>0, K_t is symmetric positive definite and its unique real symmetric logarithm gives L=−log(K_t)/t. Equality up to a permutation therefore recovers graph isomorphism. Numerical recovery can still be ill-conditioned when small eigenvalues of K_t are noisy.
extension: Study the minimum additional observations that separate this pair, such as selected off-diagonal heat entries or local clique counts. Specify whether the goal is pair separation, recovery up to isomorphism or uniformly stable reconstruction.

title: Exact modularity phases on a four-cycle
revised_question: Which graph, null model and resolution parameter define a community, and does the optimizer remain stable under perturbation?
status: Finite optimization solved exactly
summary: A small graph already exhibits resolution-dependent optima and nontrivial ties. Reporting one partition without its resolution parameter would conceal both effects.
definitions_json: ["The graph is C₄ with four edges, degree two at every vertex and total edge weight m=4.","For a vertex partition P and γ≥0, Q_γ(P)=Σ_{B∈P}[e(B)/4−γ(|B|/4)²], where e(B) counts internal undirected edges.","The feasible set contains all fifteen set partitions of four labeled vertices. Rotated partitions are distinct selections even when they have the same score."]
theorem_name: The complete modularity phase diagram
theorem_statement: For 0≤γ<1 the all-in-one partition uniquely maximizes Q_γ=1−γ. For 1<γ<2 the two partitions into adjacent pairs maximize Q_γ=1/2−γ/2. For γ>2 the singleton partition uniquely maximizes Q_γ=−γ/4. At γ=1 there are three maximizers; at γ=2 there are seven.
theorem_proof: Group partitions by block pattern and internal-edge count. Besides the three candidate lines, an adjacent pair with two singletons has score 1/4−3γ/8; a triple plus singleton has 1/2−5γ/8; opposite pairs have −γ/2; a nonadjacent pair with two singletons has −3γ/8. Comparison of these finitely many affine functions gives the envelope above. The first two candidate lines meet at γ=1. The pair and singleton lines meet at γ=2, where the four adjacent-pair-plus-singletons partitions also tie. No discarded line is higher for γ≥0. The verifier independently enumerates the partitions and evaluates rational scores at interior and boundary values.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"At γ=3/2, compare the all-in-one, adjacent-pair and singleton candidates.","calculation":"Their scores are −1/2, −1/4 and −3/8 respectively. Exactly two adjacent-pair partitions win. At γ=2 each has score −1/2, as do the four one-pair partitions and the all-singleton partition.","conclusion":"The preferred community structure changes under the chosen scale even though the graph has not changed. Boundary multiplicities are mathematically part of the answer."}
limits: This solves one finite instance, not general modularity maximization. Numerical graph algorithms may miss ties, and graph perturbations require a separate sensitivity analysis.
extension: For a weighted graph, compute the exact upper envelope of all partition score lines for manageable n. Identify parameter intervals with a unique optimizer and certify a score gap that bounds stability to weight perturbations.

title: Ensemble assumptions determine the spectral baseline
revised_question: Which random-matrix ensemble matches the dependence and normalization of the matrix being analyzed?
status: Moment calculation proved
summary: A random-matrix comparison must preserve dependence, centering and normalization. A simple fourth-moment calculation shows why a sparse adjacency matrix cannot be treated as a dense Wigner matrix without qualification.
definitions_json: ["Let A be a simple random graph on n vertices with independent Bernoulli(p) upper-triangular entries and zero diagonal.","Set W_{ij}=(A_{ij}−p)/sqrt(np(1−p)) for i≠j and W_{ii}=0. Then E W_{ij}=0 and E W_{ij}²=1/n.","A sample covariance S=XᵀX/m is positive semidefinite and belongs to a different ensemble, even if X has independent entries."]
theorem_name: Exact second and fourth normalized moments
theorem_statement: E[Tr(W²)/n]=(n−1)/n. Moreover E[Tr(W⁴)/n]=2(n−1)(n−2)/n²+(n−1)[1−3p(1−p)]/[n²p(1−p)]. Thus p=c/n with fixed c>0 yields fourth-moment limit 2+1/c, whereas np(1−p)→∞ removes this extra term.
theorem_proof: Expand the traces as sums over closed walks. For the second moment, each of n(n−1) directed edges contributes 1/n. For length four, centering kills walks containing an edge used only once. Two distinct edges traversed twice give two families of n(n−1)(n−2) walks, each with expectation 1/n². Alternating repeatedly on one edge gives n(n−1) walks with E W_{ij}⁴=[1−3p(1−p)]/[n²p(1−p)]. Divide by n to obtain the formula. This derivation depends on upper-triangular independence; it fails for matrices whose entries share hidden common factors.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare dense p=1/2 with p=c/n and compare W with a covariance matrix.","calculation":"The dense fourth-moment limit is two. The sparse fourth-moment limit retains 1/c. A covariance matrix satisfies xᵀSx=||Xx||²/m≥0, while centered symmetric adjacency matrices can have negative eigenvalues.","conclusion":"One observed eigenvalue histogram cannot select its own null ensemble. The normalization and dependence structure must be specified before interpreting outliers."}
limits: Two moments do not prove a complete limiting spectral law. The sparse calculation demonstrates a mismatch, not a universal law for every sparse network. No prediction about human behavior follows from these moment identities.
extension: Estimate the dependence and degree heterogeneity that a null ensemble must preserve. Compare centered, variance-normalized and degree-corrected matrices, and use moment or resolvent bounds matched to each construction.

title: A reversible q-dependent chain with an exact gap
revised_question: Can a q-dependent chain be defined with valid probabilities and a computable invariant distribution?
status: Finite family solved analytically
summary: Here q has one explicit meaning: the upward jump rate of a reflecting birth-death chain. This produces an actual probability model, stationary distribution and spectral answer.
definitions_json: ["The states are 0,…,N. From i<N the jump i→i+1 has rate q>0; from i>0 the jump i→i−1 has rate one.","The generator Q has diagonal entries equal to minus its outgoing rate and row sums zero. The process is irreducible on this finite state space.","Write Z=Σ_{i=0}^N qⁱ and π_i=qⁱ/Z. At q=1 this is uniform."]
theorem_name: Stationary distribution and complete nonzero spectrum
theorem_statement: Detailed balance holds, and the eigenvalues of −Q are zero and λ_k=q+1−2sqrt(q)cos(kπ/(N+1)), k=1,…,N. The spectral gap is λ_1>0.
theorem_proof: For each adjacent pair, π_i q=π_{i+1}; summing these balances proves πQ=0. Conjugate −Q by diag(sqrt(π_i)) to obtain a symmetric tridiagonal matrix S with off-diagonal −s, s=sqrt(q), interior diagonal q+1 and endpoint diagonals q and one. The interior eigenvalue recurrence has solutions v_i=sin((i+1)θ)−s⁻¹sin(iθ) for λ=q+1−2s cosθ. The left endpoint condition holds directly. The right endpoint reduces to (2cosθ−s−s⁻¹)sin((N+1)θ)=0. Taking θ=kπ/(N+1), 1≤k≤N, gives N independent nonzero eigenmodes; the stationary mode sqrt(π) supplies zero. These N+1 eigenvectors exhaust the dimension.

Exact determinant evaluation and balance checks in verify.py reproduce all three. At q=1 the gap is 2−2cos(π/(N+1)), asymptotic to π²/(N+1)².","conclusion":"The parameter has a measurable effect on equilibrium concentration and mixing, with no unspecified q-randomness."}

title: Continuous q-Hermite polynomials through a Jacobi operator
revised_question: Which operator is diagonalized by which polynomial family, with respect to what positive measure?
status: Classical family with exact low-degree verification
summary: A recurrence with positive coefficients constructs a spectral measure and explains orthogonality. This is a precise operator-polynomial connection rather than a generic appeal to q-special functions.
definitions_json: ["Fix 0<q<1. Let H₀=1, H₁=2x and H_{n+1}=2xH_n−(1−qⁿ)H_{n−1}.","On ℓ² of the nonnegative integers, define a bounded self-adjoint Jacobi operator J by off-diagonal entries a_n=sqrt(1−qⁿ)/2 for n≥1 and zero diagonal.","Let μ_q be the probability spectral measure of J at e₀. Since ||J||≤1, its support lies in [−1,1]."]
theorem_name: Orthogonality and exact norms
theorem_statement: The recurrence gives H_n(J)e₀=Π_{j=1}^n sqrt(1−qʲ)e_n. Hence ∫H_mH_n dμ_q=δ_{mn}Π_{j=1}^n(1−qʲ). In particular μ_q has second moment (1−q)/4 and fourth moment (1−q)(2−q−q²)/16.
theorem_proof: The spectral theorem identifies integration of a polynomial with its matrix element at e₀. Induct on n using 2Je_n=sqrt(1−q^{n+1})e_{n+1}+sqrt(1−qⁿ)e_{n−1}; the recurrence cancels the lower basis vector. Orthogonality then follows from orthogonality of e_n, and the norm is the squared coefficient product. For moments, count weighted return walks of length two and four from zero. At length two there is one path; at length four the paths 0→1→0→1→0 and 0→1→2→1→0 contribute a₁⁴ and a₁²a₂².
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take q=1/2 and compute H₀ through H₅ using rational coefficients.","calculation":"The probability measure has moments μ₂=1/8 and μ₄=5/128. Exact weighted-walk moments verify every pairing of H₀,…,H₅; squared norms begin 1,1/2,3/8,21/64. The finite computation does not numerically approximate an infinite oscillatory integral.","conclusion":"A recurrence, an operator and a measure now support the same calculation. The cited family name is backed by a fully stated normalization."}
limits: The Jacobi construction proves the displayed orthogonality; it does not itself reproduce every q-difference identity or special-function representation. Changing q outside the stated interval may change positivity or moment determinacy.

title: A graph game with explicit equilibria
revised_question: What are the players, strategy sets, information and payoff functions, and which perturbation changes the equilibrium set?
status: Finite equilibria and potential verified
summary: A graph becomes a game only after strategies and payoffs are supplied. The four-cycle coordination example also separates a local equilibrium from a globally optimal configuration.
definitions_json: ["Each vertex of C₄ chooses s_i∈{0,1}. Its payoff is the number of neighbors choosing the same value, minus εs_i.","A pure Nash equilibrium permits no strictly profitable unilateral change. Indifference is allowed.","The potential is Φ(s)=Σ_{edges {i,j}}1[s_i=s_j]−εΣ_i s_i."]
theorem_name: An exact potential and a perturbation-induced equilibrium change
theorem_statement: Every unilateral payoff change equals the corresponding change in Φ. At ε=0 there are six pure equilibria: the two constant profiles and the four rotations of 0011. For 0<ε<2 only the two constant profiles remain; for ε>2 only all-zero remains.
theorem_proof: Changing s_i changes exactly the edge agreement terms incident to i and its own action cost, proving the potential identity. Since the game is finite, any sequence of strict improving moves terminates. To classify C₄ equilibria, observe that at ε=0 an isolated action has two disagreeing neighbors and can improve, while blocks of two have one agreeing and one disagreeing neighbor and are weakly stable. These give exactly the listed profiles. If 0<ε<2, a boundary vertex choosing one has one neighbor of each type, so switching to zero saves ε without losing agreement. Thus mixed profiles cannot be equilibria. The constant-one profile stays stable until its cost exceeds the loss of two agreements. Constant-zero is stable for every positive ε.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Enumerate all sixteen action profiles and each of their four possible unilateral flips.","calculation":"The verifier finds six, two and one equilibria at ε=0,1/2,3 respectively and checks the potential identity for every profile and deviation at ε=1/2. At ε=0, 0011 is an equilibrium with two agreeing edges, while the global optimum has four.","conclusion":"Local stability, global optimization and a graph partition are three distinct notions. A small action cost can remove weak equilibria without changing the graph."}

extension: Characterize strict equilibria on a general graph through neighbor majorities, then compare them with potential maximizers. For constrained interventions, optimize which action costs or edge weights eliminate a selected undesirable equilibrium.

title: Relative entropy along a finite Markov chain
revised_question: Which entropy or relative entropy is monotone under the specified dynamics, and what distribution serves as equilibrium?
status: Contraction proved with a strict counterexample for Shannon entropy
summary: Relative entropy has a robust monotonicity property relative to a stationary reference distribution. The unqualified claim that any diffusion must increase Shannon entropy is false.
definitions_json: ["Let P be a row-stochastic matrix on a finite state set and π a stationary probability with every π_i>0.","D(p||π)=Σ_i p_i log(p_i/π_i), with 0log0=0. The next distribution is pP.","Shannon entropy is H(p)=−Σ_i p_i log p_i and depends on the chosen state representation."]
theorem_name: Data processing gives D(pP||π)≤D(p||π)
theorem_statement: The inequality holds for every initial distribution p. If P is doubly stochastic, it implies H(pP)≥H(p) by taking π uniform. Without this extra structure, Shannon entropy can decrease.
theorem_proof: Form joint arrays a_{ij}=p_iP_{ij} and b_{ij}=π_iP_{ij}. Their relative entropy is Σ_i p_i log(p_i/π_i), because each row of P sums to one. Summing out i sends the arrays to pP and πP=π. Apply the log-sum inequality separately in each column, then add over j. Equality in a column requires the ratios p_i/π_i to be constant among its positive incoming transitions. In particular a strictly positive P gives strict contraction unless p=π. The uniform-reference identity D(p||u)=log n−H(p) proves the doubly stochastic corollary.

Meanwhile relative entropy decreases from log(5/3)≈0.510826 to zero. The transition probabilities are exact rationals; only the displayed logarithms are numerical.","conclusion":"Convergence toward a concentrated equilibrium can reduce Shannon entropy without contradicting information contraction."}

Detailed balance produces −(1/2)Σ_{ij}π_iQ_{ij}(r_i−r_j)(log r_i−log r_j)≤0, r_i=p_i/π_i. A log-Sobolev inequality would strengthen this to a quantitative entropy-decay rate.

title: Neat groups and a smooth modular-curve example
revised_question: What does neatness ensure for Γ acting on D, and which singularities can still occur after compactification?
status: Definition clarified; rank-one example derived
summary: Neatness removes finite-order eigenvalue phenomena in an arithmetic group. It controls the open quotient, while boundary smoothness remains a separate geometric issue.
definitions_json: ["An element is neat when the multiplicative subgroup generated by its complex eigenvalues contains no nontrivial root of unity. A group is neat when each of its elements is.","For N≥3, let Γ(N)={γ∈SL₂(Z):γ≡I mod N}, acting on the upper half-plane H by fractional linear transformations.","Write Y(N)=Γ(N)∖H, using the image of Γ(N) in PSL₂(R) when discussing effective actions and indices."]
theorem_name: Γ(3) has a free action on H and its quotient is a smooth noncompact curve
theorem_statement: For γ=I+3A∈Γ(3), determinant one implies Trγ=2−9det A. Consequently the possible elliptic integer traces are excluded except the identity/unipotent trace two case. Γ(3) is neat in its defining two-dimensional representation and acts freely on H.
theorem_proof: The identity det(I+3A)=1+3TrA+9detA yields TrA=−3detA. A real SL₂ matrix fixing a point of H is elliptic; an integer elliptic trace lies in {−1,0,1}, apart from the central finite-order endpoints. None is congruent to two modulo nine, and −I has trace −2 and is absent. Nonidentity trace-two unipotents have no interior fixed point. Hyperbolic eigenvalues λ,λ⁻¹ have |λ|≠1, so their generated subgroup has no nontrivial torsion; unipotents contribute only eigenvalue one. Proper discontinuity and absence of stabilizers make the quotient smooth. This argument is specific and does not replace the general theorem that arithmetic groups contain neat finite-index subgroups.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compute Γ(3)’s effective index and cusp data.","calculation":"SL₂(F₃) has 24 elements, so the effective PSL₂ index is twelve. There are four cusps, each of width three. The torsion-free genus relation 2g−2+c=μ/6 then gives g=0 for the smooth compactification X(3). The verifier directly enumerates determinant-one residue matrices.","conclusion":"The open curve is smooth and hyperbolic, yet its compactification is genus zero. These properties are compatible."}
limits: Torsion-free and neat are distinct notions in general linear groups; their coincidence in this rank-one calculation must not be generalized indiscriminately. Smoothness of the open quotient alone does not determine the geometry of a chosen higher-dimensional boundary.
extension: For a specified higher-rank group, compare level conditions that guarantee neatness with cone decompositions that guarantee regular toroidal charts. These are two separate certificates.

title: Minimal and toroidal compactifications in an explicit chart
revised_question: Which compactification preserves which properties, and where do choices enter?
status: Curve case constructed; higher-dimensional distinction stated
summary: In dimension one the basic boundary operation is tangible: a punctured disk acquires its missing point. Higher-dimensional toroidal compactification adds combinatorial choices that this curve example does not see.
definitions_json: ["A cusp of width N has local translation τ↦τ+N. The invariant coordinate is q_N=exp(2πiτ/N).","For Imτ sufficiently large, the cusp quotient is a punctured disk 0<|q_N|<ε. Adding q_N=0 gives a smooth disk.","For an arithmetic quotient of a Hermitian symmetric domain, the Baily–Borel construction supplies a canonical projective completion. Toroidal constructions use admissible rational cone decompositions near boundary components."]
theorem_name: The rank-one cusp fills smoothly, but a fan can create or resolve toric singularities
theorem_statement: The smooth compactification of a modular curve fills each cusp with one point; the normal curve completion is unique. In higher dimensions, a toroidal boundary chart is smooth only when its relevant cones are regular in the chosen lattice. Projectivity requires a compatible support-function condition rather than following from any arbitrary subdivision.
theorem_proof: The q_N coordinate is unchanged by τ↦τ+N and maps a horizontal fundamental strip at large imaginary height bijectively to a punctured disk. The puncture can be filled by the standard complex coordinate. In one complex dimension normality already implies smoothness, which explains why the minimal/toroidal distinction is muted for curves. To see a genuinely higher-dimensional local issue, take a two-dimensional cone generated by (1,0),(1,2). Its primitive generators have determinant two, so the affine toric chart is singular. Inserting the ray (1,1) gives two determinant-one cones and hence smooth charts. This is a local toric illustration, not an assertion that this fan is the fan of a particular unstated arithmetic quotient.

The fan computation changes a singular affine chart into a smooth toric modification. The two calculations demonstrate two distinct roles for boundary construction.","conclusion":"Canonical completion, smoothness and projectivity must be checked individually; they are not synonyms for making a space richer."}

title: General type and log-general type on modular curves
revised_question: For which group, level and compactification is the canonical divisor big, and what boundary corrections enter?
status: Curve family calculated; higher-dimensional problem bounded
summary: The canonical divisor of a compactification and the log-canonical divisor of its punctured interior answer different questions. Principal modular curves make the difference explicit without appealing to vague increases in structure.
definitions_json: ["For a smooth projective curve X of genus g, deg K_X=2g−2. It is of general type exactly when g≥2.","For a reduced divisor D of c punctures, deg(K_X+D)=2g−2+c. The open curve is of log-general type exactly when this is positive.","For N≥3, the effective principal congruence group has index μ_N=|SL₂(Z/NZ)|/2, all cusp widths N, and c_N=μ_N/N. There are no elliptic points."]

theorem_statement: For X(3), μ=12, c=4 and g=0. Thus deg K=−2 but deg(K+D)=2. For X(7), μ=168, c=24 and g=3, so deg K=4 and deg(K+D)=28. Both interiors are log-general type, but only the latter compact curve is general type.
theorem_proof: A torsion-free index-μ quotient of the upper half-plane has hyperbolic area μπ/3, because PSL₂(Z) has area π/3. Gauss–Bonnet on the surface with c cusps gives area 2π(2g−2+c), so 2g−2+c=μ/6. Since every cusp has width N, the cusp-width sum gives c=μ/N. These equations calculate g. On a compact curve, a divisor is big exactly when its degree is positive: Riemann–Roch makes its large multiples grow linearly with positive leading coefficient, whereas nonpositive degree cannot have that growth. Applying this to K and K+D proves the distinction. The verifier directly counts determinant-one matrices modulo N for N=3,…,7 and recovers genera 0,0,0,1,3.

It lies between the genus-zero and general-type compact examples.","conclusion":"A precise level-dependent calculation replaces the unsupported inference that smoothness or hyperbolicity already implies a big canonical divisor."}

title: A projective embedding from a degree bound
revised_question: Which additional structure turns the particular analytic space into an algebraic or projective one?
status: Curve criterion proved from Riemann–Roch
summary: Projectivity can be demonstrated by producing enough sections of a line bundle to separate points and tangent directions. The curve case gives a concrete replacement for a list of named geometric structures.
definitions_json: ["Let X be a smooth projective curve over C of genus g and L a line bundle of degree d.","A line bundle is very ample when its complete linear system gives a closed embedding into projective space.","Riemann–Roch says h⁰(L)−h⁰(K_X⊗L⁻¹)=d+1−g. A line bundle of negative degree has no nonzero section."]
theorem_name: Degree at least 2g+1 guarantees a projective embedding
theorem_statement: If d≥2g+1, then h⁰(L)=d+1−g and L separates points and tangent vectors. Hence its complete linear system embeds X into P^(d−g).
theorem_proof: For any length-two subscheme Z of X, deg(K_X⊗L⁻¹(Z))=2g−2−d+2≤−1. Serre duality therefore gives H¹(L(−Z))=0. The exact sequence 0→L(−Z)→L→L|_Z→0 shows that restriction of sections to Z is onto. Taking two distinct points gives separation of their values, and taking a double point gives tangent separation. The same argument for a length-one subscheme gives base-point freeness. These are the embedding criteria for the complete linear system. The section count follows from the vanishing of H¹(L) and Riemann–Roch. This proof states exactly which positivity replaces an unsupported claim of projectivity.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take a genus-one curve and a line bundle of degree three.","calculation":"The bound is met, h⁰(L)=3, and the resulting embedding is into P² with degree three: a smooth plane cubic. For g=3 and d=7, there are five sections and an embedding into P⁴. These are actual dimensions of spaces of sections, not a metaphorical richness measure.","conclusion":"A concrete line bundle can turn an abstract curve into an explicit projective object. Algebraic descriptions and projective embeddings are nevertheless distinct notions."}
limits: The argument begins with a smooth projective curve and does not prove that every analytic space is algebraizable. An algebraic affine line already shows that being algebraic need not mean being projective. Higher-dimensional embedding criteria require their own positivity and vanishing results.
extension: For a particular analytic compactification, identify a candidate line bundle, prove its positivity, obtain the required sections and show that their map is injective and immersive. State separately any algebraization theorem used to enter the algebraic category.

revised_question: In which projective space does a smooth hypersurface of degree d have trivial canonical bundle?
status: Canonical bundle and characteristic classes computed
summary: The phrase two-dimensional Calabi–Yau quintic was not a sufficiently defined geometric object. Adjunction determines which degree and ambient dimension actually produce trivial canonical bundle.
