title: A quadratic program with singular cases included
revised_question: What is the exact optimizer, when is it unique, and how do additional constraints change it?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: The positive-definite inverse formula is only one branch of the quadratic-program problem. The singular case admits a clean complete classification, and inequality constraints can change the optimizer even when the matrix is nonsingular. These are mathematical statements about quadratic forms, not practical allocation recommendations.
definitions_json: ["Let Σ be a symmetric positive semidefinite real matrix and c≠0. Minimize wᵀΣw subject to cᵀw=1. Write Σ⁺ for its Moore–Penrose inverse and kerΣ for its nullspace."]
theorem_name: Complete equality-constrained PSD classification
theorem_statement: If some z∈kerΣ has cᵀz≠0, the minimum is zero and all minimizers are the feasible null vectors. Otherwise c∈rangeΣ, q=cᵀΣ⁺c>0, the minimum is 1/q, and all minimizers are Σ⁺c/q+z with z∈kerΣ.
theorem_proof: In the first case, z/(cᵀz) is feasible and has zero objective; positive semidefiniteness rules out a lower value. In the second case, c is orthogonal to the nullspace and hence lies in the range. Set w₀=Σ⁺c/q. It is feasible and Σw₀=c/q. For any feasible w=w₀+h, cᵀh=0, so the cross term 2hᵀΣw₀ vanishes and the objective is 1/q+hᵀΣh. Equality holds exactly when h∈kerΣ. This also proves uniqueness precisely when the feasible tangent space contains no nonzero null vector.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare a diagonal matrix, a rank-one matrix, and a nonnegative constraint.","calculation":"For Σ=diag(1,4), c=(1,1), w*=(4/5,1/5) and the minimum is 4/5. For Σ=11ᵀ, every feasible w has objective one. For Σ=[[1,2],[2,9]], the unrestricted optimizer is (7/6,−1/6) with value 5/6; imposing w≥0 gives (1,0) with value one. Its KKT multiplier for the second coordinate is positive.","conclusion":"Nullspaces, budgets and inequality constraints must be handled together; merely replacing an inverse by a pseudoinverse does not cover every singular case."}
limits: If Σ is indefinite the convex proof fails and the objective may be unbounded below along feasible directions. Additional bounds or penalties define different programs.
extension: For rational inputs, produce exact KKT and nullspace certificates, then study the parameter loci where the active set or nullspace changes.

title: Open-system dynamics must preserve physical states
revised_question: Does the proposed reduced evolution preserve trace, positivity and complete positivity, and under what approximation?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: An open-system equation must preserve the convex set of density operators, including when an auxiliary system is attached. An exactly solvable qubit channel provides a stronger check than inspection of trace alone. Its Kraus form supplies complete positivity directly.
definitions_json: ["A density operator is a positive semidefinite matrix ρ with trace one. A map is completely positive when its tensor product with the identity map on any finite auxiliary system preserves positivity. Set ℏ=1."]
theorem_name: Exact amplitude-damping semigroup
theorem_statement: For H=0 and L=√γ |0⟩⟨1| with γ≥0, the Lindblad equation sends ρ=[[a,b],[b*,d]] to [[a+(1−q)d,√q b],[√q b*,qd]], where q=e^(−γt), t≥0. This defines a trace-preserving completely positive semigroup.
theorem_proof: Direct matrix multiplication in LρL†−{L†L,ρ}/2 gives ḋ=−γd, ḃ=−γb/2 and ȧ=γd, which solve to the displayed formula. Define K₀=diag(1,√q) and K₁=√(1−q)|0⟩⟨1|. Their adjoint squares sum to I, and ΣK_jρK_j† reproduces the solution. Tensoring each K_j with an auxiliary identity shows complete positivity. Since q(t+s)=q(t)q(s), composition satisfies the semigroup law.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Start from |+⟩⟨+|, so a=d=b=1/2.","calculation":"At q=1/4 the output is [[7/8,1/4],[1/4,1/8]], with trace one and determinant 3/64>0. More generally detρ(t)=q detρ(0)+q(1−q)d²≥0, giving an additional two-by-two positivity check. As t tends to infinity the state approaches |0⟩⟨0|.","conclusion":"The exact solution verifies what the mathematical generator does. It does not establish that this generator describes any proposed physical mechanism."}
limits: A reduced microscopic model can require weak-coupling, coarse-graining or Markov assumptions before it has this form. Trace preservation alone is weaker than positivity, and positivity alone is weaker than complete positivity. Negative-time inversion is not a physical damping channel.
extension: Add a specified Hamiltonian or dephasing operator and test whether an exact solution, a spectral decomposition of the generator, or a controlled splitting error is available.
references_json: [{"label":"Microscopic derivation of one-qubit amplitude and phase damping Kraus operators","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.01145"},{"label":"Solution of the Lindblad equation in the Kraus representation","url":"https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.74.062113"}]

title: Population growth and the actual logarithmic time
revised_question: What initial condition is intended, what are the units of t, and what time solves the stated equation exactly?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: The original numerical claim can be resolved entirely within its assumed exponential model. The corrected answer is a model time, not a prediction of a real population. The factor of one half changes the initial condition and must not be silently discarded.
definitions_json: ["For discrete-time growth, P(t)=P₀(1+r)^t with r>−1; allowing real t is an interpolation of that formula. A continuous exponential with the same unit-step multiplier has rate λ=log(1+r), not r exactly."]
theorem_name: Exact target time and rate sensitivity
theorem_statement: For P(t)=154000(1.0005)^t/2, the starting value is 77000. The time to P*=10¹² is t*=log(10¹²/77000)/log(1.0005)=32767.109878086… in the specified time units. If only integer times are allowed, the first crossing is 32768.
theorem_proof: Take logarithms of the positive equation P*=77000(1.0005)^t. Strict monotonicity of the exponential gives a unique real solution, and integer rounding follows from the same monotonicity. For a general multiplier 1+r>1, differentiation yields ∂t*/∂r=−log(P*/P₀)/[(1+r)log(1+r)²]. This makes the long extrapolation highly sensitive to the assumed rate. Replacing log(1+r) by r is only a small-r approximation whose cumulative error should be reported.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare the stated discrete interpolation with a continuous model using λ=0.0005.","calculation":"The latter target time is log(10¹²/77000)/0.0005≈32758.92083, about 8.18905 units earlier. Substituting t*=32767.109878086 back into the original formula recovers 10¹² to the working floating-point precision. The previously reported value near 11788 does not satisfy the equation.","conclusion":"Correct arithmetic settles a question about a formula; it does not supply evidence that the formula remains valid over tens of thousands of units."}
limits: The model assumes a fixed rate and no carrying capacity, migration, stochasticity or resource constraint. Any logistic replacement needs a stated carrying capacity larger than the target, otherwise the target is never reached in finite time.
extension: Specify a bounded-growth ODE, derive its target-time formula and classify unreachable targets before computing a numerical crossing.

title: A unified equation needs shared variables and invariances
revised_question: What mathematical object is common to the models, and which transformation preserves the claimed structure?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: A useful unification identifies a common mathematical structure and proves a transportable statement. Gradient flows provide one such structure, but the metric and mobility are part of the model. Sharing an energy symbol does not make two systems dynamically equivalent.
definitions_json: ["Let E:Rⁿ→R be differentiable. A mobility K(x) is a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix. The dynamics ẋ=−K(x)∇E(x) uses the chosen Euclidean coordinates; positive-definite K defines a corresponding metric interpretation."]
theorem_name: Energy dissipation and coordinate transport
theorem_statement: Every sufficiently differentiable solution satisfies dE/dt=−∇EᵀK∇E≤0. Under an invertible linear change y=Sx, the transported energy Ẽ(y)=E(S⁻¹y) and mobility K̃(y)=SK(S⁻¹y)Sᵀ preserve this dissipation identity.
theorem_proof: The chain rule gives Ė=∇Eᵀẋ, and positive semidefiniteness gives the sign. For the coordinate change, ∇_yẼ=S⁻ᵀ∇_xE and ẏ=Sẋ=−SKSᵀ∇_yẼ. Substitution recovers the same scalar energy derivative. This calculation explains why transforming only the state while keeping an arbitrary identity mobility generally changes the dynamics. The result requires neither thermodynamic terminology nor a claim that all dissipative systems are gradient flows.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take E(x)=xᵀAx/2 with symmetric A positive semidefinite, and K=I.","calculation":"Then ẋ=−Ax and Ė=−xᵀA²x. A finite weighted-graph heat equation has this form with A equal to the graph Laplacian, while the scalar equation ẋ=−x is its one-dimensional instance. A constant component in the Laplacian nullspace is preserved rather than dissipated, which shows the difference between nonincrease and convergence to a unique state.","conclusion":"The shared theorem is energy monotonicity under a specified positive mobility. A proof of equivalence requires an actual state-space map such as S and the correctly transported energy and mobility."}
limits: Nonsymmetric transport, Hamiltonian components, constraints and nonlocal metrics require extensions. Energy decrease alone does not prove boundedness, uniqueness, convergence rate or identification from observations.
extension: Separate a generator into dissipative and skew parts, prove the resulting balance law and ask which observations distinguish the mobility from the energy.

title: Bessel versus Parseval
revised_question: What assumptions yield an inequality, and what extra completeness makes it an equality?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: The missing distinction in the original inequality list is completeness. Bessel’s inequality is an exact statement about projection error; Parseval’s equality appears when the chosen orthonormal family spans the relevant Hilbert space. A residual formula makes the practical meaning immediate.
definitions_json: ["Use an inner product linear in its first argument. For an orthonormal family e₁,…,e_m, define P_mx=Σ⟨x,e_j⟩e_j. Its span is a closed finite-dimensional subspace of the Hilbert space H."]
theorem_name: Projection residual and completeness criterion
theorem_statement: For every x, ||x||²=Σ_{j=1}^m|⟨x,e_j⟩|²+||x−P_mx||². For a countable orthonormal family, the infinite coefficient sum is at most ||x||². Equality for every x holds exactly when its closed linear span is H.
theorem_proof: The residual is orthogonal to every e_j because taking its inner product with e_j subtracts the same coefficient. Pythagoras therefore splits the norm into projection and residual, and orthonormality gives the coefficient sum. Finite partial sums are increasing and bounded, so their limit exists. The partial projections form a Cauchy sequence, with squared differences equal to sums of omitted squared coefficients. Their limit projects onto the closed span. Equality means the residual projection onto the orthogonal complement vanishes. If equality holds for all x, that complement is zero and the span is dense.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take x=(2,3,6) in R³ and initially observe only e₁,e₂.","calculation":"The observed squared coefficient sum is 4+9=13, total squared norm is 49, and residual squared norm is 36. Adding e₃ removes the residual exactly. Omitting e₃ never becomes harmless merely because the first two coefficients were calculated to high precision.","conclusion":"This is both an approximation certificate and a statement of what the measurement family cannot see."}
limits: An infinite orthonormal family need not be complete. For nonorthogonal features, coefficients from raw inner products are not automatically orthogonal projections, and frame or Gram-matrix analysis is needed.
extension: Develop a frame analogue with lower and upper frame bounds, or identify the cheapest observation family whose residual vanishes on a specified finite-dimensional model class.

title: Hölder and Young with equality cases
revised_question: Which conjugate exponents apply, and when is the bound sharp?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: Conjugate exponents and equality cases turn a generic inequality into a sharp tool. The proof below also states what must be checked before applying it: measurability, the relevant integrability and the distinction between the absolute-value bound and the signed integral.
definitions_json: ["Let 1<p<∞ and q=p/(p−1), so 1/p+1/q=1. Norms are ||f||_p=(∫|f|^p)^(1/p) and the analogous q-norm, on one fixed measure space."]
theorem_name: Young and Hölder with sharp equality
theorem_statement: For a,b≥0, ab≤a^p/p+b^q/q, with equality exactly when a^p=b^q. Consequently ∫|fg|≤||f||_p||g||_q. For nonzero finite norms, equality holds exactly when |f|^p/||f||_p^p=|g|^q/||g||_q^q almost everywhere.
theorem_proof: Fix a and minimize h(b)=b^q/q−ab+a^p/p over b≥0. Its derivative is b^(q−1)−a, with its unique minimum at b=a^(p−1), and the minimum equals zero. Normalize nonzero f,g to unit p- and q-norms, apply the scalar inequality pointwise and integrate. Equality in the integrated nonnegative difference requires pointwise equality almost everywhere, which yields the normalized-power condition. To obtain equality for |∫fg| as well, the product must also have an almost-everywhere constant phase or sign.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Choose p=3, q=3/2, a=2 and b=4.","calculation":"Here a^p=b^q=8, so Young is exact: ab=8=8/3+8/(3/2). For a finite counting measure, proportional normalized powers supply equally explicit Hölder equality examples. Choosing disjointly supported nonzero functions makes the product integral zero while both norms are positive, showing a strict case.","conclusion":"The equality condition identifies when a proposed estimate is sharp and which directions are responsible for slack."}
limits: The endpoints p=1,q=∞ require essential-supremum language and a different equality statement. If either required norm is infinite, the finite useful estimate is unavailable even when a formal product expression can be written.
extension: Use the equality characterization to optimize a linear functional on an L^p unit ball and compare existence and uniqueness in endpoint versus strictly convex cases.

title: Matrix norms and the quantity being bounded
revised_question: Which matrix norm corresponds to the input and output errors being measured?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: Choosing a norm means choosing how input and output error are measured. A norm catalogue becomes useful only when attached to its induced error inequality. A two-dimensional example shows that several plausible norms report different numerical amplification.
definitions_json: ["The induced p-norm is ||A||_p=sup_{x≠0}||Ax||_p/||x||_p. The induced 1-norm is the largest absolute column sum, the induced infinity-norm is the largest absolute row sum, and the Frobenius norm is a Euclidean norm on entries."]
theorem_name: Sharp induced bounds and singular-value comparisons
theorem_statement: For every vector x, ||Ax||_p≤||A||_p||x||_p. In Euclidean norm, ||A||₂ is the largest singular value, while ||A||_F² is the sum of squared singular values; hence ||A||₂≤||A||_F≤√r||A||₂ for rank r>0.
theorem_proof: The first inequality is the definition of the supremum. For p=1, triangle inequalities bound each output coordinate and collecting each |x_j| gives the maximum column sum; choosing a coordinate vector at a maximizing column attains it. The infinity case uses a maximizing row and matching signs. Orthogonal or unitary invariance reduces the Euclidean claims to a diagonal singular-value matrix, where the largest entry bounds their squared sum above and below. The rank-zero case has both norms zero.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Let A=[[1,2],[0,1]].","calculation":"Its induced 1- and infinity-norms are both three. Its Frobenius norm is √6. The eigenvalues of AᵀA=[[1,2],[2,5]] are 3±2√2, so ||A||₂=√(3+2√2)=1+√2. These are distinct measures of the same operator. A claim of amplification three is sharp for a 1-norm or infinity-norm question, but overestimates the sharp Euclidean factor.","conclusion":"Reporting the input and output norms is part of stating the bound, not a cosmetic implementation detail."}
limits: Condition numbers also depend on the norm and require invertibility or a specified pseudoinverse/restricted subspace. An entrywise norm cannot replace an induced one without tracking the comparison constants.
extension: For a chosen observation map, compute the restricted operator norm on the admissible state subspace and quantify how much a generic full-space bound overestimates the actual errors.

title: Lyapunov conditions in the right direction
revised_question: What sufficient conditions prove stability or decay, and what actually follows when those sufficient conditions fail?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: A Lyapunov certificate is a sufficient argument tied to a chosen function. Failure of one function is not a system-instability certificate. The exact example below resolves that logical error and produces a contracting quadratic geometry for the same stable system.
definitions_json: ["For ẋ=Ax and symmetric P, define V(x)=xᵀPx. Positive definiteness P≻0 makes V comparable with ||x||². Along a trajectory, V̇=xᵀ(AᵀP+PA)x. A Hurwitz matrix has all eigenvalues in the open left half-plane."]
theorem_name: Quadratic certificate and a counterexample to the failed converse
theorem_statement: If P≻0 and AᵀP+PA=−Q with Q≻0, then V(t)≤exp(−λ_min(Q)t/λ_max(P))V(0), proving exponential stability. A stable A can nevertheless make d||x||²/dt positive at some state.
theorem_proof: The derivative identity follows by the product rule. Since xᵀQx≥λ_min(Q)||x||² and V≤λ_max(P)||x||², V̇≤−[λ_min(Q)/λ_max(P)]V. Integration gives exponential decay of V; the lower eigenvalue bound on P translates this into a Euclidean state bound. The proof makes no assertion that every positive function has a negative derivative. For Hurwitz A, the integral P=∫₀∞exp(tAᵀ)Qexp(tA)dt provides the converse existence result, with convergence following from exponential matrix decay.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take A=[[-1,4],[0,−1]], whose eigenvalues are both −1.","calculation":"At x=(1,1), Ax=(3,−1) and d(xᵀx)/dt=2xᵀAx=4>0. Yet P=[[1/2,1],[1,9/2]] has positive leading minor and determinant 5/4, and direct multiplication gives AᵀP+PA=−I. Thus the Euclidean norm can temporarily grow while the certified P-norm decreases.","conclusion":"The apparent contradiction disappears once the certificate is interpreted in the right direction and its metric is stated."}
limits: A certificate for one linearization is not automatically a global nonlinear proof. Semidefinite Q needs an invariance argument for asymptotic convergence, and strict inequalities matter near marginal modes.
extension: Find a common quadratic Lyapunov function for a specified family of matrices, or exhibit why switching among individually stable matrices defeats a proposed common bound.

title: Units of the Einstein equation
revised_question: In which coordinates or orthonormal frame are component units being stated, and how do both sides match?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: Dimensional statements about tensor components must name the coordinate or frame convention. Using a local orthonormal frame and x⁰=ct makes the audit simple, while also explaining why coordinate components in other charts can carry different units.
definitions_json: ["Use metric signature (−,+,+,+), spacetime coordinates of length dimension, and a dimensionless orthonormal metric. Write G_N for Newton’s constant, c for speed, ε for energy density and G_μν for the Einstein tensor; the two symbols G have unrelated types."]

theorem_statement: In this convention G_μν and Λg_μν have dimensions L⁻²; T_μν has dimensions ML⁻¹T⁻². Since [G_N]=L³M⁻¹T⁻² and [c⁴]=L⁴T⁻⁴, (G_N/c⁴)T_μν has dimension L⁻². The factor 8π is dimensionless and is not selected by dimensional analysis.
theorem_proof: A connection coefficient contains one derivative of a dimensionless metric, giving L⁻¹, and curvature has a derivative of the connection or a product of two connections, giving L⁻². Energy per volume is (ML²T⁻²)/L³=ML⁻¹T⁻². Multiplying exponents in G_N c⁻⁴T gives zero mass exponent, length exponent −2 and zero time exponent. The cosmological constant must have the same curvature dimension when it multiplies the dimensionless metric. All statements are frame and coordinate dependent at the component level, while the tensor equation is geometric.

If instead time is represented by t rather than ct, changing the coordinate basis introduces c factors into the time components; one must transform the tensor rather than recycle the orthonormal component units.","conclusion":"The repaired equation is G_μν+Λg_μν=(8πG_N/c⁴)T_μν. title: Why the coefficient is 8π
revised_question: Which weak-field matching fixes the dimensionless coefficient that units cannot determine?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: The coefficient 8π is determined by matching a conventioned relativistic field equation to Newtonian Poisson gravity. The trace reversal supplies a crucial factor one half. This is a derivation of the classical normalization, not a new gravitational law.
definitions_json: ["Set Λ=0 for the local weak-field limit. Use signature (−,+,+,+), x⁰=ct and R^ρ_{σμν}=∂_μΓ^ρ_{νσ}−∂_νΓ^ρ_{μσ}+Γ^ρ_{μα}Γ^α_{νσ}−Γ^ρ_{να}Γ^α_{μσ}, with R_σν=R^ρ_{σρν}. Let G_μν=κT_μν initially have an unknown κ."]
theorem_name: Newtonian matching yields κ=8πG_N/c⁴
theorem_statement: For a static weak potential with g_00=−(1+2Φ/c²), slow matter and negligible pressure, R_00≈∇²Φ/c² and the trace-reversed source is T_00−g_00T/2≈ρc²/2. Matching ∇²Φ=4πG_Nρ therefore gives κ=8πG_N/c⁴.
theorem_proof: Contract the field equation in four dimensions: −R=κT. Substituting back gives R_μν=κ(T_μν−g_μνT/2). For dust at rest, T_00≈ρc², spatial diagonal stresses are negligible, and T≈−ρc²; with g_00≈−1 the displayed source becomes ρc²−ρc²/2. The weak, static connection is Γ^i_{00}≈∂_iΦ/c². In R_00, time derivatives vanish and connection products are higher order, leaving ∂_iΓ^i_{00}≈∇²Φ/c². Thus ∇²Φ=(κc⁴/2)ρ. Equating its coefficient with Poisson’s coefficient fixes κ.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Track the factors before inserting the answer.","calculation":"If one incorrectly equates R_00 with κρc² without trace reversal, the inferred coupling would differ by a factor of two. If one uses time rather than ct, the connection and stress components must both be rescaled. Either mistake can produce superficially plausible but inconsistent equations.","conclusion":"The numerical factor and powers of c are fixed together once geometric, matter and Newtonian conventions are stated."}
limits: This leading-order derivation assumes weak fields, slow motion, small stresses and a regime in which Λ is negligible. Reversing the Riemann-tensor sign requires changing the field-equation sign convention consistently. The result does not derive Einstein’s equation uniquely from Newtonian gravity.

title: Sixteen entries but ten independent components
revised_question: How do index range, symmetry, differential identities and gauge freedom affect the equation count?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: There are several counts in general relativity, and conflating them produces incorrect conclusions. Matrix entries, independent tensor components, differential identities, initial-data constraints and physical propagating modes belong to different stages of the analysis.
definitions_json: ["Use indices μ,ν∈{0,1,2,3}. A symmetric covariant tensor satisfies S_μν=S_νμ. The Einstein tensor obeys four contracted Bianchi identities. In a 3+1 formulation, the spatial metric and its conjugate momentum have six components each."]
theorem_name: Component count and local vacuum degree-of-freedom count
theorem_statement: A symmetric four-by-four tensor has ten independent components: four diagonal and six off-diagonal. The four contracted Bianchi identities are differential identities, not four duplicate entries. For regular vacuum general relativity, four first-class constraints acting on twelve spatial canonical variables leave four physical phase-space variables, or two configuration polarizations per spatial point.
theorem_proof: For an n-by-n symmetric matrix there are n diagonal entries and n(n−1)/2 unordered off-diagonal pairs, giving n(n+1)/2. At n=4 this is ten, although the full display contains sixteen slots. The Bianchi relations differentiate combinations of field-equation components; they do not identify any selected four slots algebraically. In the canonical count, a first-class constraint imposes one phase-space condition and generates one gauge direction. Four such constraints therefore remove eight of the twelve spatial canonical variables. Dividing the remaining four phase-space variables into coordinate-momentum pairs gives two local propagating degrees of freedom.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Write the first row as S_00,S_01,S_02,S_03 and the remaining rows with S_10=S_01 and the corresponding symmetries.","calculation":"There is no S_44 in the chosen zero-through-three convention. A one-through-four convention may use it, but mixing the two is invalid. In a linearized plane-wave gauge, the remaining transverse-traceless amplitudes can be represented by h_+ and h_×, illustrating rather than replacing the constrained Hamiltonian count.","conclusion":"The repaired statement retains all ten independent equations while explaining their differential dependence and gauge structure."}
limits: Boundary conditions, global moduli, matter fields and singular constraint surfaces can affect global degrees of freedom. Subtracting four identities from ten components is not on its own a derivation of two propagating modes.
extension: Perform an explicit linearized gauge reduction for a plane wave and compare it with the canonical count in a stated background and boundary setting.

title: Covariant conservation is a structural condition
revised_question: How does the divergence identity constrain admissible source equations?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: Covariant conservation is the compatibility condition supplied by the geometry of the field equation. It does not say that coordinate components are constant, or that a global conserved total energy exists in every spacetime. A homogeneous expanding metric gives an exact example of the distinction.
definitions_json: ["For the Levi-Civita connection, ∇g=0 and the contracted Bianchi identity is ∇^μG_μν=0. Let κ and Λ be constants. A perfect fluid has rest energy density ε, pressure p and four-velocity normalized by u·u=−1 in a c=1 convention."]
theorem_name: Source conservation and the FLRW continuity equation
theorem_statement: The field equation G_μν+Λg_μν=κT_μν with κ≠0 implies ∇^μT_μν=0. In a homogeneous FLRW metric, this includes ε̇+3H(ε+p)=0, where H=ȧ/a. For constant equation-of-state parameter p=wε, εa^{3(1+w)} is constant.
theorem_proof: Apply the covariant divergence to the field equation. The geometric identity and metric compatibility eliminate the left side, and constant κ gives the conclusion. In comoving FLRW coordinates, expanding ∇_μT^{μ0}=0 combines the ordinary time derivative of ε with the connection terms associated with the changing spatial volume a³; isotropic pressure contributes three identical work terms. Substitution p=wε yields d logε/dt=−3(1+w)d loga/dt, whose integral gives the power law wherever ε and a are positive.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare dust and radiation under a scale factor that doubles.","calculation":"For dust w=0, energy density falls by 2³=8. For radiation w=1/3, it falls by 2⁴=16. Neither changing component violates covariant conservation. The additional radiation factor expresses the pressure-work or redshift contribution in this model.","conclusion":"A conservation law can involve geometric transport and changing volume. Ordinary component constancy is not the right test."}
limits: A global conserved charge generally needs an appropriate symmetry or boundary construction. If κ or Λ varies, additional derivative terms enter and the simple inference must be revised. Matter models must satisfy their own evolution equations consistently.
extension: Given a Killing field ξ, derive conservation of J^μ=T^{μν}ξ_ν for symmetric covariantly conserved T, and identify the boundary conditions needed to turn it into a constant integrated charge.

title: Grothendieck universes and their logical cost
revised_question: Which closure axioms are needed, and what additional set-theoretic assumption supports the chosen universe?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: Universe language is a relative-size discipline backed by a set-theoretic assumption. It is not a mechanism for eliminating every paradox without cost. The useful mathematical task is to state the closure axioms and show exactly which categorical constructions they permit.
definitions_json: ["A Grothendieck universe U is a transitive set closed under pairing, power sets and unions indexed by a set belonging to U, with the family’s members in U. To support ordinary infinite mathematics one asks ω∈U. A U-small set is an element of U, which differs from merely being a subset of U."]
theorem_name: The inaccessible-cardinal construction of a universe
theorem_statement: If κ is a strongly inaccessible cardinal, then V_κ is a Grothendieck universe containing ω. Consequently U-small sets, maps, finite products and function sets can be handled inside one fixed relative-size level. The existence of such an uncountable inaccessible cardinal is an additional assumption, not a theorem of bare ZFC.
theorem_proof: Transitivity of the cumulative hierarchy is immediate. If x,y∈V_κ, their ranks are below κ, so pairing and power sets still have rank below κ because κ is a limit ordinal. For an indexed family (x_i)_{i∈I} with I∈V_κ, strong inaccessibility ensures every set in V_κ has cardinality below κ. Regularity then bounds the supremum of the fewer-than-κ ranks of x_i below κ, so their union remains in V_κ. For function sets X→Y, their graphs are subsets of X×Y and are therefore contained in a suitable iterated power-set construction inside U.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take two U-small sets X and Y.","calculation":"Ordered pairs can be constructed by the Kuratowski definition, yielding X×Y∈U. Every function graph lies in P(X×Y), and the collection of all such graphs is a subset of that power set, hence U-small under the closure axioms. By contrast, the entire collection of all U-small sets is U itself; asserting U∈U would contradict foundation. It belongs to a larger universe only when another size assumption is made.","conclusion":"The construction makes size bookkeeping precise while retaining a visible logical boundary."}
limits: This treatment proves the conditional construction, not consistency or existence of inaccessible cardinals. Degenerate finite universes and conventions excluding or including ω must be distinguished. Different foundational treatments can avoid universe axioms for specific constructions.
extension: Rebuild one category-of-structures construction using a fixed cardinal bound instead, then compare its smallness guarantees with the universe-based version.
references_json: [{"label":"SGA 4 Exposé I universes and strongly inaccessible cardinals","url":"https://grothendiecksga.com/read/sga4/en/I-A-5.html"},{"label":"Stacks Project constructing categories of schemes","url":"https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/000H"}]

title: Stirling partitions do not supply torsional energy
revised_question: What physical or combinatorial equivalence relation is being counted, and what energy or probability weights make that count relevant?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: The original torsion comparison combined two unrelated notions of structure: set partitions and elastic deformation. Both can be developed, but a counting theorem does not determine an energy. An explicit discrete energy and continuum limit provide the missing bridge when an actual rod model is intended.
definitions_json: ["S(N,k) counts partitions of N labeled objects into k nonempty unlabeled subsets. A contiguous partition of an ordered chain instead cuts k−1 of its N−1 gaps. For a rod of length L, θ(x) is an angular displacement and GJ>0 is a torsional stiffness parameter."]
theorem_name: Distinct partition counts and a consistent torsional energy
theorem_statement: Arbitrary partitions satisfy S(N,k)=kS(N−1,k)+S(N−1,k−1); contiguous k-block partitions number C(N−1,k−1). For grid spacing h=L/N, E_N=(GJ/2)Σ_{i=0}^{N−1}[(θ_{i+1}−θ_i)/h]²h equals the continuum Dirichlet energy of the piecewise-linear interpolant.
theorem_proof: For Stirling’s recurrence, the last label either joins one of k existing blocks or forms a singleton. For contiguous partitions, choosing the cut gaps is a bijection. For energy, the interpolant derivative is constant on each grid interval and equals the difference quotient; integrating its squared derivative gives the formula exactly. Thus strong H¹ convergence of interpolants implies energy convergence. A bounded-energy sequence with a fixed endpoint has an H¹ bound; weak lower semicontinuity gives a lower energy bound at weak limits, while interpolating smooth functions supplies elementary recovery approximations. No set-partition count is needed for this argument.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"First take N=4,k=2, then a constant total twist Θ.","calculation":"The partition counts are seven and three respectively. For θ_i=Θi/N, every difference quotient is Θ/L and E_N=GJΘ²/(2L) for every N. For L=GJ=1 and θ(x)=x², endpoint interpolation gives E_N=2/3−1/(6N²), converging to (1/2)∫₀¹4x²dx=2/3.","conclusion":"The continuum energy follows from a stated stiffness law and interpolation, not from taking a limit of the Stirling numbers."}
limits: The one-dimensional quadratic energy assumes a chosen linear elastic model. Material nonlinearities, warping, varying stiffness and topology of configurations require additional specification. Algebraic torsion in a group is a different concept again.
extension: If partitions represent actual latent material domains, define a weighted sum over contiguous partitions with a stated domain energy and examine its continuum or large-system limit.

title: Vector motion and rotation conventions
revised_question: How do local movement commands map into world coordinates, and when does diagonal input change speed?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: Movement commands can be formulated without ambiguous appeals to trigonometry. Linear algebra combines the local commands; a rotation converts the resulting vector into another frame. Keeping magnitude conventions explicit resolves diagonal-speed discrepancies.
definitions_json: ["In a right-handed plane use column vectors and counterclockwise rotation R(θ)=[[cosθ,−sinθ],[sinθ,cosθ]]. Let a local command u=(u₁,u₂) specify components in orthonormal local axes. World velocity is v=su rotated by R, namely v=sR(θ)u."]
theorem_name: Rotation preserves speed but raw diagonal input changes it
theorem_statement: Because RᵀR=I, ||v||₂=s||u||₂. A single unit-axis command has speed s, while raw input u=(1,1) has speed s√2. Normalizing nonzero input by its Euclidean norm produces constant speed s regardless of its direction.
theorem_proof: Multiply the displayed matrix by its transpose and use cos²θ+sin²θ=1 and cancellation of the cross terms. Taking squared norms then gives the identity. The difference between axis and diagonal commands follows from ||(1,0)||=1 and ||(1,1)||=√2. If the desired control preserves analog intensity below unit radius, the mapping u↦u/max(1,||u||) leaves small commands unchanged and caps only those outside the unit disk. This is a specified control law, not a consequence forced by coordinate geometry.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Use the exact rotation with cosθ=3/5 and sinθ=4/5.","calculation":"The unit forward command maps to (3/5,4/5), of squared norm one. The unnormalized diagonal maps to (−1/5,7/5), of squared norm two. Its normalized version divides both components by √2, returning squared norm one. These checks use exact rational arithmetic before the final normalization.","conclusion":"Coordinate conversion and speed policy can be independently tested. This makes it possible to change a frame without silently changing the physical or numerical interpretation of commands."}
limits: Nonorthogonal coordinate bases, perspective projection, acceleration limits and a non-Euclidean metric alter the formula or the appropriate norm. Time-dependent frames introduce additional derivative terms when differentiating positions.
extension: Specify an anisotropic metric or acceleration constraint, then derive the admissible velocity set and a frame-consistent control projection onto it.

title: A proposed analogy needs a dimensionless correspondence
revised_question: Is there an actual operator correspondence with matched units, spectra and observables?
status: Classical result developed and worked
summary: A spectral analogy becomes mathematical only when state spaces, operators, units and observables are related by an explicit map. A small periodic hopping model supplies a genuine Bloch calculation, while a similarity-transform example separates shared eigenvalues from shared dynamics.
definitions_json: ["Consider a two-site unit cell on an infinite one-dimensional lattice with real hoppings t₁,t₂. Its Hermitian Bloch matrix is H(k)=[[0,t₁+t₂e^(−ik)],[t₁+t₂e^(ik),0]], where k is a dimensionless crystal phase. Hopping parameters and eigenvalues have a common energy unit."]
theorem_name: An explicit band gap and a warning about spectral equivalence
theorem_statement: The two bands are E_±(k)=±√(t₁²+t₂²+2t₁t₂cosk). Their minimum separation is 2||t₁|−|t₂||. Equality of eigenvalue sets in another model does not establish equivalence of observation maps or Euclidean amplification.
theorem_proof: The characteristic polynomial is E²−|t₁+t₂e^(−ik)|². Expanding the squared modulus gives the dispersion relation. Its minimum is (|t₁|−|t₂|)² because cosk ranges over [−1,1]. If B=SAS⁻¹, A and B share characteristic polynomials, but exp(tB)=S exp(tA)S⁻¹ and Euclidean norm bounds acquire the condition number of S. Only a unitary S preserves every Euclidean norm and the inner-product structure automatically. Observables must also transform, for example C_B=C_A S⁻¹, to preserve measured outputs.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take t₁=2,t₂=1 and compare an unrelated rescaled two-state model.","calculation":"The bands at k=0 are ±3 and at k=π are ±1, so the gap is two. To transfer this statement, another model must supply a compatible periodic operator, an energy-scale conversion and a map respecting the relevant measurements. A match between an energy number and some unrelated flux number has no meaning until units and maps are supplied.","conclusion":"This example yields an actual operator theorem and a precise test for proposed cross-domain correspondences."}
limits: The toy model does not establish that another physical system has Bloch periodicity, the same Hilbert space or the same operator domain. Isospectral operators can remain distinguishable by eigenvectors, locality and response functions.
extension: Classify intertwiners BS=SA that also preserve a chosen observation map, and determine which spectral or transport identities survive after taking dimensionless variables.

title: Residual energy and exact Gaussian calibration
revised_question: Is the intended quantity a residual energy, a standardized discrepancy or an information divergence?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: The original squared-deviation formula becomes useful once its units, reference model and covariance are specified. A squared residual is a geometric discrepancy. An entropy is a functional of a probability distribution. Neither name determines the other.
definitions_json: ["Let r=X−μ∈Rᵈ. The raw residual energy is E=rᵀr. If Σ is a specified positive-definite covariance, the whitened discrepancy is Q=rᵀΣ⁻¹r.","Here μ and Σ are known constants under the null model, rather than estimates obtained from the same observations."]
theorem_name: Whitened Gaussian discrepancy
theorem_statement: If X has multivariate normal distribution N(μ,Σ) with Σ positive definite, then Q has the χ² distribution with d degrees of freedom. Consequently E[Q]=d and Var(Q)=2d. The unweighted E generally depends on the coordinate units.
theorem_proof: Factor Σ=LLᵀ with L invertible and put Z=L⁻¹r. The change-of-variables formula gives independent standard normal coordinates Z₁,…,Z_d. Then Q=ZᵀZ=ΣZᵢ². Its moment-generating function is the product (1−2t)^(−d/2), obtained by completing the square in each one-dimensional Gaussian integral. Differentiation at zero gives the stated moments. Changing the scale of one coordinate changes E but is canceled by the corresponding covariance transformation in Q.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take r=(1,2) and Σ=diag(1,4).","calculation":"The raw residual is E=1+4=5. Whitening gives Z=(1,1), so Q=2. If both coordinates are expressed in ten times larger numerical units, r becomes (10,20) and Σ becomes diag(100,400); E becomes 500, whereas Q remains 2.","conclusion":"The standardized discrepancy is dimensionless and has an exact reference distribution under the declared Gaussian null. It has not thereby become Shannon entropy."}
limits: Estimating means, regression coefficients or covariance from the same sample changes the null distribution. In ordinary known-variance linear regression, orthogonal projection gives n−p residual degrees of freedom; estimated covariance can instead lead to F or other statistics. Nonnormal residuals need separate calibration.
extension: Study how Q changes under covariance uncertainty by bounding it between eigenvalue-controlled quadratic forms. This produces an honest robustness interval rather than assigning an entropy interpretation to a residual.

title: The chain rule as a statement about local linear maps
revised_question: Which local linear approximation is intended, and how does a coordinate change transform it?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: The derivative is the linear part of a local approximation. The chain rule composes these linear parts and tracks their domains; a secant slope or a scalar symbol does not replace a multivariable derivative.
definitions_json: ["For differentiable g:Rᵐ→Rⁿ and f:Rⁿ→Rᵏ, Dg(x):Rᵐ→Rⁿ and Df(g(x)):Rⁿ→Rᵏ are linear maps.","Differentiability means g(x+h)=g(x)+Dg(x)h+o(||h||), with the remainder small relative to ||h||."]
theorem_name: Typed chain rule
theorem_statement: D(f∘g)(x)=Df(g(x))Dg(x). If a scalar F has Hessian operator norm at most M along the segment from x to x+h, its linearization remainder is at most M||h||²/2.
theorem_proof: Insert the differentiability expansion of g into the expansion of f at g(x). Since g(x+h)−g(x)=O(||h||), the outer remainder is o(||h||). The coefficient of h is exactly the displayed composition. For the second statement, integrate the directional derivative along the segment twice; the second integral is ∫₀¹(1−t)hᵀH_F(x+th)h dt, whose absolute value is bounded by M||h||²/2.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Let g(u,v)=(u²+v,eᵘ) and f(a,b)=ab, so F(u,v)=(u²+v)eᵘ.","calculation":"Dg=[[2u,1],[eᵘ,0]], while Df(g)=[eᵘ,u²+v]. Multiplication gives DF=[eᵘ(2u+u²+v),eᵘ]. At (1,2), DF=(5e,e). Direct differentiation of F gives the same row vector and therefore independently checks the composition order.","conclusion":"A perturbation (h₁,h₂) changes F to first order by 5eh₁+eh₂. The two inputs have different sensitivities; one scalar slope would omit that distinction."}
limits: The Hessian remainder bound requires a neighborhood with a uniform bound. A pointwise derivative alone supplies no global finite-step error estimate. Nondifferentiable coordinate changes need different calculus.
extension: For a long computation, propagate both Jacobians and explicit remainder bounds. This distinguishes a mathematically controlled sensitivity estimate from an uncalibrated finite-difference plot.

title: Graph heat flow and the stability of a discrete gradient step
revised_question: When does a discrete gradient step decrease the energy, and which PDE is its continuous analogue?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: Heat evolution and gradient descent share a variational structure after choosing a metric and boundary conditions. Their discrete stability restrictions come from the spectrum of the actual discretized operator.
definitions_json: ["Let L be a symmetric positive-semidefinite graph Laplacian and E(x)=xᵀLx/2.","Continuous heat evolution is ẋ=−Lx. A forward Euler step is x⁺=(I−ηL)x. The constant vector is in the kernel when L is an ordinary graph Laplacian."]
theorem_name: Spectral energy decrease
theorem_statement: Continuous evolution satisfies dE/dt=−||Lx||². A discrete step is nonexpansive in Euclidean norm for every x exactly when 0≤η≤2/λ_max, assuming λ_max>0; the same interval makes E nonincreasing. Strict decay on every positive eigenspace holds for the explicit open interval 0<η<2/λ_max; η=0 produces no decay.
theorem_proof: Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis Lqᵢ=λᵢqᵢ and write x=Σcᵢqᵢ. Continuous coefficients are cᵢ(t)=e^(−λᵢt)cᵢ(0). For the step, cᵢ⁺=(1−ηλᵢ)cᵢ. Thus ||x⁺||²−||x||²=Σ[(1−ηλᵢ)²−1]cᵢ². This is nonpositive for every coefficient vector precisely when every factor has magnitude at most one. Multiplying each term by λᵢ/2 proves the energy version. Also 1ᵀx⁺=1ᵀx, so mass is preserved independently of decay.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Use the four-cycle Laplacian with eigenvalues 0,2,2,4.","calculation":"For η=0.4, the update factors are 1,0.2,0.2,−0.6, hence every nonconstant mode contracts. For η=0.6, the largest-frequency factor is −1.4 and that mode grows. The equilibrium constant mode remains unchanged in both cases.","conclusion":"A large time step can turn a dissipative differential equation into an unstable numerical scheme. Continuous dissipation alone cannot certify the discretization."}
limits: Energy monotonicity does not imply positivity of each coordinate. Positivity of forward Euler is governed by entrywise update weights and can require a smaller bound. Nonsymmetric operators require a different argument.
extension: Compare forward, backward and exponential steps for a common graph, recording preservation of mass, positivity and decay separately.

title: Exact exponent arithmetic before approximation
revised_question: What exact exponent and mantissa follow from the expression, and what relative error does an approximation make?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: Very large magnitudes are best handled by separating an exact exponent from a modest mantissa. That separation avoids overflow and makes errors in scale immediately visible.
definitions_json: ["Scientific notation writes a positive number as a×10ᵏ with 1≤a<10.","Relative error for an approximation ỹ to y≠0 is |ỹ−y|/|y|. A decimal logarithm adds log₁₀a to the exponent."]
theorem_name: Square-root normalization
theorem_statement: For an integer m and a>0, √(a×10^(2m))=√a×10ᵐ. For the recovered expression, √(5×10^54004)=√5×10^27002 exactly.
theorem_proof: Both factors on the right are positive, and squaring gives 5×10^(2×27002), which is the original radicand. Uniqueness of the positive square root completes the proof. If an exponent is odd, move one factor of 10 into the mantissa before taking the square root; there is no need to evaluate the enormous number itself.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Approximate the exact answer by 10^27002, or instead retain eleven significant mantissa digits.","calculation":"The exact logarithm is 27002+(log₁₀5)/2. Omitting √5 gives relative error 1−1/√5≈0.5527864045, over 55 percent. Keeping 2.2360679775 as mantissa gives a small rounding error whose size can be bounded by squaring rational decimal endpoints around √5. The old comparison with 25,000×10^50,000 differs by tens of thousands of decimal orders.","conclusion":"An order-of-magnitude summary and a numerical approximation answer different questions. Stating the exact exponent costs essentially no extra computation."}
limits: Exponent manipulations assume the usual positive real square root. Complex powers require a branch convention, and expressions with uncertain exponents need interval propagation rather than a single rounded exponent.
extension: Use rational interval endpoints for the mantissa and retain an integer exponent in all later products, quotients and roots. This gives a small certificate that can be replayed without arbitrary-precision libraries.

title: Competing response laws and identifiable parameters
revised_question: Which experimental quantity, input scale and noise model would distinguish the proposed functional laws?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: A named empirical law is a family of fitted functions with a domain and an error model. A rigorous mathematical comparison first asks whether the parameters and competing shapes can be distinguished at all.
definitions_json: ["For x>0, a power response is y=axᵇ with a>0. Its logarithm is log y=α+b log x, α=log a.","An additive Gaussian model for y and an additive Gaussian model for log y imply different likelihoods. Hick-type logarithmic response models use a different independent variable and cannot be substituted without defining the experiment."]
theorem_name: Two-point identifiability in the noiseless power family
theorem_statement: For two distinct positive inputs x₁≠x₂ and positive outputs, there is a unique power-law interpolant: b=log(y₂/y₁)/log(x₂/x₁) and a=y₁/x₁ᵇ. This identifies a family member, not the truth of the family.
theorem_proof: Taking logarithms makes the problem a two-equation linear system with design rows (1,log x₁) and (1,log x₂). Its determinant log(x₂/x₁) is nonzero, so the solution is unique. A third input is therefore already an opportunity to reject the noiseless family rather than simply refit its two parameters. title: Tensor order and matrix rank are different invariants
revised_question: Does rank mean tensor order, matrix rank or minimum number of decomposable terms?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: A second-order tensor may be represented by a matrix, but its order is not the number of nonzero eigenvalues. A dyadic decomposition adds a third meaning of rank that needs a stated field and symmetry convention.
definitions_json: ["For a real matrix A, rank(A) is the dimension of its image. A rank-one dyad uvᵀ maps x to u(vᵀx).","For a real symmetric A, the spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis and A=Σλᵢvᵢvᵢᵀ. Negative coefficients are permitted in this signed decomposition."]

theorem_proof: The image of a sum of r rank-one maps is contained in the span of their r output vectors, so its rank is at most r. Therefore at least rank(A) summands are necessary. The spectral theorem supplies exactly rank(A) nonzero signed symmetric dyads. Finally every sum Σcᵢvᵢvᵢᵀ with cᵢ≥0 has nonnegative quadratic form, so an indefinite matrix cannot possess such a decomposition.

Replacing the zero entry by ε≠0 changes rank to three even when ||A_ε−A||₂=|ε| is arbitrarily small.","conclusion":"Exact rank is discontinuous at a rank-deficient matrix; numerical effective rank requires a declared threshold and noise scale."}

title: A fully normalized spin one-half Wigner representation

status: Developed classical result with worked example

definitions_json: ["Write A=a₀I+a·σ, with Pauli matrices σ=(σ_x,σ_y,σ_z). For Hermitian A, the four coefficients are real.","Choose Δ(n)=(I+√3 n·σ)/2 for unit n∈S² and measure dμ=dΩ/(2π), whose total mass is two. Define W_A(n)=Tr(AΔ(n))."]

Expanding W_AΔ and integrating leaves a₀I+a·σ. Expanding W_AW_B gives 2a₀b₀+2a·b, exactly Tr(AB). These calculations also fix the measure normalization; using dΩ/(4π) without changing other factors would break reconstruction.

The six directions ±e_x,±e_y,±e_z with weights 1/3 each reproduce all required spherical moments exactly, so the reconstruction and trace identity can be checked by a six-point sum.","conclusion":"Negativity is compatible with reconstruction because Δ(n) is not a positive measurement effect. title: Exact polynomial Moyal products
revised_question: What star product is being used, on what function class or formal series ring, and which limit recovers the Poisson bracket?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: On polynomial symbols the Moyal exponential terminates, so one can verify noncommutativity and associativity with exact arithmetic rather than relying on an informal infinite series.
definitions_json: ["For canonical coordinates (q,p), let B=←∂_q→∂_p−←∂_p→∂_q and define f⋆g=Σₙ≥₀(iℏ/2)ⁿBⁿ(f,g)/n!.","For polynomials only finitely many differentiated terms survive. The corresponding formal-series definition can be used beyond polynomials without claiming analytic convergence."]

theorem_proof: At first order q⋆p=qp+iℏ/2 and p⋆q=pq−iℏ/2; higher derivatives vanish. Interchanging f and g changes the sign of B, so only odd n contribute to the commutator. After division by iℏ, the n=1 term is the Poisson bracket and the next possible term has order ℏ². For associativity, introduce three tensor factors. The constant-coefficient bidifferential operators B₁₂, B₁₃ and B₂₃ commute. Either parenthesization is ordinary multiplication after exp[(iℏ/2)(B₁₂+B₁₃+B₂₃)], establishing equality.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Set ℏ=1 and take f=q², g=p².","calculation":"The finite expansion gives q²⋆p²=q²p²+2iqp−1/2, while p²⋆q²=q²p²−2iqp−1/2. Their commutator is 4iqp, agreeing with i times {q²,p²}=4qp. The verifier also compares both parenthesizations for a family of low-degree monomials with rational complex coefficients.","conclusion":"The example checks a finite, exact algebra. It requires no discretized phase-space grid and therefore has no grid-resolution error."}
limits: Formal associativity does not prove convergence of the Moyal series for arbitrary smooth functions. Trace-integral identities require integrability and boundary conditions; polynomial symbols on the full plane are usually not integrable.

title: A spectral definition of fractional quantum evolution

definitions_json: ["On the circle of length 2π, use normalized Fourier modes e_n(x)=e^(inx)/√(2π). For α>0, define (−Δ)^(α/2)e_n=|n|^αe_n.","Take ℏ=1 and H=D_α(−Δ)^(α/2) with D_α>0. Its domain consists of coefficients satisfying Σ|n|^(2α)|c_n|²<∞."]

Exponentiation multiplies each coefficient by a complex number of modulus one. Parseval therefore gives ||ψ(t)||²=Σ|c_n|². Multiplying by the same unchanged spectral weights proves energy conservation for states in the form domain.

The coefficients at time t are (1,e^(−it),e^(−i2√2t))/√3, so their squared magnitudes still sum to one. At α=2 the energies become 0,1,4; this is a change in dispersion, not a change of normalization.","conclusion":"The finite-mode example can be replayed exactly at the spectral level and numerically in physical space."}

title: Lagrange identity and its equality geometry
revised_question: Which identity is intended and what assumptions justify its use in the proposed field calculation?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: The finite-dimensional identity is an exact decomposition of the Cauchy–Schwarz deficit. An operator boundary identity sharing the same historical name is a separate theorem with separate domains.
definitions_json: ["For a,b∈Rⁿ, define the antisymmetric coordinate minors m_ij=a_i b_j−a_j b_i.","The exterior product a∧b has squared norm Σ_{i<j}m_ij² in the orthonormal exterior basis."]

The cross terms contribute −Σ_ij a_i a_j b_i b_j=−(a·b)². If a≠0 and every minor vanishes, select an index i with a_i≠0. The identities a_i b_j=a_j b_i give b=(b_i/a_i)a. If a=0, dependence is immediate.

The three minors are −5,−2,11, whose squares sum to 25+4+121=150. In three dimensions this is also ||a×b||².","conclusion":"The identity quantifies the area spanned by two vectors; it does not itself introduce a field equation or an elasticity model."}

title: Winding number and Gauss–Bonnet with boundaries explicit
revised_question: Which invariant is defined for the actual object, and which deformations preserve it?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: Topological charges are attached to specified spaces and deformation classes. Winding number and Euler characteristic are both invariant quantities, but they are not interchangeable measurements of a generic defect.
definitions_json: ["For a closed C¹ loop z:[0,2π]→C∖{0}, the winding number is w=(1/(2πi))∫z′(t)/z(t)dt.","For a closed oriented smooth surface, Gauss–Bonnet states ∫K dA=2πχ. A surface with boundary needs a boundary-geodesic-curvature term and possible corner contributions."]

The radial integral vanishes because r has equal endpoints. Since the loop closes, θ(2π)−θ(0) is an integer multiple of 2π. Under a zero-avoiding homotopy, the resulting winding is continuous in the homotopy parameter and integer-valued, hence constant. Smooth approximation extends the argument to continuous loops.

title: An explicit marked-torus deformation
revised_question: What marked surface, deformation class and metric or functional make the proposed optimization well defined?

definitions_json: ["For τ in the upper half-plane, the marked complex torus is C/(Z+τZ). The marking identifies the two chosen lattice generators with a fixed reference basis.","A quasiconformal map has f_z̄=μf_z with |μ|<1 almost everywhere. For a real-linear orientation-preserving map its maximal dilatation is K=(1+|μ|)/(1−|μ|)."]

The real singular values are 1 and b, giving the same K as their ratio. For optimality among maps in the marking class, the standard extremal-length distortion bound applied to horizontal and vertical curve families gives K at least max(b,1/b); this affine map attains it. The extremal-length bound is the classical geometric input, not a consequence merely of the algebraic derivative calculation.

title: Certified first logistic-map period doublings
revised_question: Which bifurcation parameters are being approximated, and what evidence supports a claimed scaling limit?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: The first two bifurcation parameters can be obtained algebraically, so they provide exact calibration points before any numerical Feigenbaum-ratio experiment.
definitions_json: ["Let f_r(x)=rx(1−x), with r in [0,4] and x in [0,1]. A period-k orbit is stable when the absolute value of the derivative of f_r^k along it is less than one.","A flip bifurcation is detected when this multiplier passes through −1, subject to the usual nondegeneracy conditions."]

theorem_statement: The nonzero fixed point x*=1−1/r loses linear stability at r₁=3. The genuine two-cycle, existing for r>3, has multiplier m₂=−r²+2r+4 and is stable for 3<r<1+√6. Its roots are x_±=(r+1±√((r−3)(r+1)))/(2r), giving multiplier −r²+2r+4 by their sum and product. The equation m₂=−1 selects r₂=1+√6, with derivative −2√6≠0. To check the flip nondegeneracy rather than infer birth from the multiplier alone, let g=f_r² near one cycle point. The logistic Schwarzian is Sf=−6/(1−2x)², and Sg=(Sf∘f)(f′)²+Sf<0 on the threshold cycle, where both first derivatives are nonzero. At g′=−1, the cubic normal-form coefficient is g‴/6+(g″)²/4=−Sg/6>0. Transversality and this positive coefficient are the hypotheses of the classical supercritical flip theorem. The algebra verifies those hypotheses; the local bifurcation theorem is classical input.

Therefore 3.449489742783178<r₂<3.449489742783179. At r=3.2 the multiplier is 0.16; at r=3.5 it is −1.25, independently locating stability and instability.","conclusion":"The first low-order thresholds are now exact benchmarks, not points inferred from a bifurcation picture."}

title: Parameter loci, orbit closures and dissipative flows

definitions_json: ["For z₀=0 and zₙ₊₁=zₙ²+c, the Mandelbrot set is the set of parameters c whose critical orbit remains bounded.","The Lorenz vector field is ẋ=σ(y−x), ẏ=x(ρ−z)−y, ż=xy−βz. Its state space is R³; σ,ρ,β are separate parameters."]

For the flow, the diagonal derivatives are −σ,−1,−β. Liouville’s formula for the derivative flow gives det DΦ_t=exp(−(σ+1+β)t) while the solution exists. This controls transported volume, not orbit separation in every direction.

For c=1 it begins 0,1,2,5 and then escapes by the criterion. The Lorenz volume factor is exp(−41t/3), regardless of ρ; this cannot alone distinguish periodic from chaotic parameter regimes.","conclusion":"A bounded critical orbit and a contracting state-space volume are statements about different objects and require different evidence."}

title: Convex conjugates with their actual domains
revised_question: What is the function’s domain, when is the supremum finite and how is the original function recovered?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: A Legendre–Fenchel transform is a supremum over a declared domain. Solving a derivative equation is sufficient only after boundary and finiteness cases are checked.
definitions_json: ["For an extended-real function f:R→R∪{+∞}, f*(p)=sup_x(px−f(x)). A domain restriction is encoded by f=+∞ outside the domain.","Fenchel’s inequality says f(x)+f*(p)≥px. Equality holds exactly when p is a subgradient of a closed proper convex f at x."]

For the exponential, differentiating gives eˣ=p, so p>0 has the unique maximizer x=logp. If p=0, the supremum of −eˣ is zero but is approached only as x→−∞. If p<0, sending x→−∞ makes px−eˣ diverge to +∞. These cases prove the complete extended-real formula.

The same stationary equation cannot be used unchanged in both domains. For eˣ at p=0, no finite maximizer exists despite a finite conjugate value.","conclusion":"The example distinguishes finite supremum, attainment and an interior critical point."}

title: The CHSH bound and a finite-sample test

title: An exact free resolution and a separate geometric blowup
revised_question: Is the requested output a complex of free modules or a smooth space with a proper birational map?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: A free resolution records relations among polynomial generators. A resolution of singularities changes a geometric space by a birational morphism. The two constructions can inform one another but their outputs and correctness criteria are different.
definitions_json: ["Let R=k[x,y] and I=(x²,xy,y²). Define d₀:R³→I by d₀(a,b,c)=ax²+bxy+cy².","Let d₁:R²→R³ have columns s₁=(−y,x,0) and s₂=(0,−y,x). With grading, the complex is 0→R(−3)²→R(−2)³→I→0."]
theorem_name: A minimal graded free resolution of I
theorem_statement: The displayed complex is exact, and its entries lie in the homogeneous maximal ideal, so it is minimal as a graded free resolution.
theorem_proof: First d₀s₁=d₀s₂=0. Suppose ax²+bxy+cy²=0. Reducing modulo x gives c≡0 modulo x, so c=xc₁. Dividing by x gives ax+by+c₁y²=0. Reducing modulo y gives a≡0 modulo y; write a=−ya₁. Then b=xa₁−yc₁. Thus (a,b,c)=a₁s₁+c₁s₂, proving equality of image and kernel. If u s₁+v s₂=0, the first coordinate gives yu=0 and the last gives xv=0, so u=v=0 because R is a domain. This proves injectivity. The standard graded minimality criterion applies since no differential entry is a unit.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Compare the plane cusp y²=x³ over a field of characteristic zero.","calculation":"In the blowup chart y=xv, the total transform is x²(v²−x)=0. The strict transform v²−x=0 is smooth because its derivative with respect to x is −1. Its parametrization x=v²,y=v³ gives the familiar normalization map. It remains tangent to the exceptional divisor x=0; a normal-crossings embedded resolution requires further work.","conclusion":"The syzygy calculation proves exactness of a module complex. The blowup calculation proves smoothness of a strict transform in the relevant chart. Neither should be described as the other."}
limits: The one-chart cusp example is not a general resolution algorithm or a completed embedded normal-crossings calculation. Schreyer methods do not automatically supply the geometric blowup data.
extension: Construct a separate certificate for each stage of an embedded resolution, including exceptional multiplicities and intersection behavior.

title: A complete two-dimensional toric subdivision
revised_question: Which cone is singular, and which subdivision produces regular cones while preserving the required map?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: A rational cone contains enough combinatorial data to detect and resolve a simple affine toric singularity. The lattice, primitive generators and subdivision must be specified rather than inferred from a picture.
definitions_json: ["Use N=Z² and the cone σ generated by v₀=(1,0),v₂=(1,2). A full-dimensional two-dimensional cone is regular when its primitive ray generators form a lattice basis.","The affine toric variety is Spec C[σ∨∩M], where M is the dual lattice. Subdividing a cone without changing its support defines a proper birational toric morphism."]
theorem_name: Regular subdivision of an index-two cone
theorem_statement: The original cone has determinant two and is singular. Adding the primitive ray v₁=(1,1) divides it into two determinant-one cones, giving a smooth toric surface mapping properly and birationally to the original affine surface.
theorem_proof: The determinant det(v₀,v₂)=2 is the index of their generated sublattice. The adjacent determinants det(v₀,v₁)=det(v₁,v₂)=1, so both charts have ray bases of N and are smooth. The fan has the same support and agrees with the original torus, establishing properness and birationality by the standard toric fan criterion. The dual semigroup is generated by (0,1),(1,0),(2,−1), with the relation (0,1)+(2,−1)=2(1,0). Hence the original coordinate ring is C[u,v,w]/(uw−v²), whose gradient vanishes at the origin.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Calculate the determinant and ring descriptions directly.","calculation":"The defining polynomial F=uw−v² has gradient (w,−2v,u), so the only complex singular point is the origin. Each subdivided chart is a polynomial two-variable chart because its ray basis is unimodular. The exceptional curve records the new ray and is contracted by the toric morphism.","conclusion":"This supplies a full combinatorial smoothness certificate for this fan and a concrete algebraic model of the singular target."}
limits: A determinant test at one cone does not establish smoothness of every cone in a larger fan. Properness depends on support and fan compatibility, not only local determinants.
extension: Implement a two-dimensional subdivision certificate that checks primitive rays, angular ordering, unchanged support and determinant one for every resulting cone.

title: Hodge numbers constrained by geometry
revised_question: Which variety, smoothness assumptions, coefficient field and cohomology theory support the proposed Hodge diamond?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: A Hodge diamond is meaningful only after choosing a cohomology theory and geometric hypotheses. Smooth projective complex examples provide exact checks of both the numbers and their symmetries.
definitions_json: ["For a smooth projective complex variety X, h^(p,q)=dim H^q(X,Ω_X^p) and b_k=Σ_{p+q=k}h^(p,q).","For a smooth connected projective complex curve of genus g, the only nonzero Hodge numbers are h^(0,0)=h^(1,1)=1 and h^(1,0)=h^(0,1)=g."]
theorem_name: Curve and product examples
theorem_statement: A genus-g curve has Betti numbers (1,2g,1) and Euler characteristic 2−2g. For P¹×P¹ the nonzero Hodge numbers are h^(0,0)=h^(2,2)=1 and h^(1,1)=2, giving Euler characteristic four.
theorem_proof: For curves, holomorphic one-forms have dimension g, and complex conjugation gives the antiholomorphic dimension g. Connectedness and orientation give the degree-zero and degree-two classes. Summing along diagonals proves the Betti numbers. For P¹, the Hodge polynomial is 1+uv. The Künneth formula for the product gives (1+uv)²=1+2uv+u²v², from which all displayed Hodge numbers follow. Their alternating total agrees with the product of the two sphere Euler characteristics.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Use an elliptic curve and a smooth plane quintic.","calculation":"At g=1, the elliptic curve has Betti numbers (1,2,1) and χ=0. A smooth plane curve of degree d has genus (d−1)(d−2)/2 by adjunction; at d=5 this gives g=6, hence Betti numbers (1,12,1) and χ=−10. This also independently diagnoses the earlier confusion between a plane quintic curve and a quintic Calabi–Yau threefold.","conclusion":"The numbers are linked by proven geometric structure, rather than predicted merely from a name or a numerical pattern."}
limits: Singular, nonproper or non-Kähler examples require modified statements; ordinary pure Hodge symmetries cannot be assumed unchanged. Numerical estimates are not exact Hodge-number certificates.
extension: For a specified smooth hypersurface, compute its relevant graded Jacobian pieces and reconcile the resulting Hodge numbers with independent Euler and symmetry checks.

title: A rational parametrization and a nonexistence certificate
revised_question: Which point set is sought, and what certifies completeness rather than a bounded search?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: Finding many points and proving a point set complete are different achievements. Elementary conics already show how parametrization, integer constraints and local obstructions lead to distinct certificates.
definitions_json: ["For an equation X defined over Q, X(Q) is the rational point set, X(Z) the integral point set and X(F_p) a reduction over a finite field when defined.","Clearing denominators in a rational point yields a primitive integer tuple; primitivity must be retained in divisibility arguments."]
theorem_name: Two conic certificates
theorem_statement: Every rational point of x²+y²=1 except (−1,0) is x=(1−t²)/(1+t²), y=2t/(1+t²) for t∈Q. The conic x²+y²=3 has no rational point.
theorem_proof: For the circle, draw the line y=t(x+1) through (−1,0). Substitution factors out the known intersection and yields the displayed second point. Conversely, for a rational circle point with x≠−1, t=y/(x+1) is rational and reconstructs the point, proving completeness. For x²+y²=3, a rational point would yield primitive integers a,b,c with a²+b²=3c². Modulo three, squares are zero or one; their sum can be zero only when a and b are divisible by three. Substituting a=3a₁,b=3b₁ gives c²=3(a₁²+b₁²), so c is also divisible by three, contradicting primitivity.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Set t=2 for the parametrized circle.","calculation":"This gives x=−3/5,y=4/5 and verifies the equation exactly. By contrast no finite search is needed for the second conic: the divisibility contradiction rules out every rational denominator at once. Its lack of integer points also follows from squares modulo four, but that easier integer argument alone would not automatically prove the rational statement.","conclusion":"A complete parametrization and a nonexistence proof are both finite certificates, though of different kinds."}
limits: Local solvability is not a general guarantee of global rational solvability for arbitrary varieties. A bounded search with no point is not itself a nonexistence theorem.
extension: Choose a higher-degree curve and state exactly which global theorem or height bound would turn a point search into a complete result.

title: A typed glossary that prevents invalid compositions
revised_question: Which objects and operations do the symbols denote in the problem currently being solved?
status: Developed classical result with worked example
summary: A useful glossary is attached to one mathematical argument. Recording domains, codomains, fields and adjoints prevents expressions that look symbolic but cannot be composed or interpreted consistently.
definitions_json: ["Use F:R²→R, g:R³→R², DF(g(x)):R²→R and Dg(x):R³→R². Their composition DF(g(x))Dg(x):R³→R is well typed.","Over C, Aᵀ denotes transpose and A† conjugate transpose. They serve different bilinear and Hermitian pairings."]
theorem_name: Type correctness and positivity are substantive conditions
theorem_statement: The matrix product rule requires the inner dimensions to match. A complex squared norm is z†z, not zᵀz. The latter can vanish for a nonzero vector, so substituting transpose for adjoint can invalidate a positivity argument.
theorem_proof: An m×n matrix represents a map from n-dimensional coordinate vectors to m-dimensional vectors. Composition A∘B is represented by AB when B has matching output dimension n; coordinate expansion proves the familiar summation over the shared index. For positivity, z†z=Σ|z_i|² is real and nonnegative, and equals zero only at z=0. In contrast zᵀz is a complex bilinear expression whose terms can cancel. These are algebraic differences, not stylistic notation choices.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take z=(1,i) and a derivative composition with DF=[2,3], Dg=[[1,0,4],[0,1,5]].","calculation":"Here zᵀz=1+i²=0 although z is nonzero, whereas z†z=2. The derivative product is [2,3,23], a 1×3 row representing a map R³→R. Reversing the factors is not even dimensionally defined. The checker verifies the legal product and rejects incompatible dimensions.","conclusion":"A short typed glossary can therefore expose a false proof before any sophisticated theorem is invoked."}
limits: Matching dimensions is necessary but not sufficient: boundedness, differentiability, measurability, convergence and geometric compatibility may also be required. A formal type checker cannot silently supply them.
extension: Attach assumptions and units to the same signatures, then propagate them through a complete worked calculation so every invoked theorem has a visible hypothesis ledger.

title: Bernstein–Sato certificates and a minimality proof
revised_question: For which polynomial f can we calculate its b-function and verify the functional equation explicitly?
status: Classical result developed and example checked
summary: The original broad application question becomes an exact operator identity with a lower-bound argument. A certificate proves that a polynomial works; minimality proves that it is the b-function. Both steps can be completed for monomials, and a linear coordinate change supplies a nonmonomial example.
definitions_json: ["Work over C in the Weyl algebra generated by x and ∂ with ∂x−x∂=1. The parameter s commutes with both generators.","A Bernstein–Sato relation is P(s)f^(s+1)=b(s)f^s in the formal localization module. The global b-function is the monic polynomial of least degree satisfying such a relation."]
theorem_name: Exact monomial b-function
theorem_statement: For m≥1, b_(x^m)(s)=∏_(j=1)^m(s+j/m), with certificate P(s)=m^(−m)∂^m.
theorem_proof: Differentiate x^(m(s+1)) exactly m times. The coefficient is ∏_(k=0)^(m−1)(m(s+1)−k)=m^m∏_(j=1)^m(s+j/m), proving the certificate. To prove minimality, put an arbitrary polynomial-coefficient operator in normal order Σ a_ij(s)x^i∂^j. Its action contributes the Laurent monomial x^(ms+m+i−j). The coefficient of x^(ms) can only receive terms with j=m+i. Every such falling-factorial coefficient contains all m factors from the displayed certificate. The other Laurent powers are independent over C(s), so any possible b(s) is divisible by that monic product. Thus the candidate is minimal, not merely an annihilating multiple.
worked_example_json: {"setup":"Take f=x²y³ and then the nonmonomial f=x²+y².","calculation":"For x²y³, P=(1/108)∂ₓ²∂ᵧ³ gives b(s)=(s+1/2)(s+1/3)(s+2/3)(s+1)². The same exponent-comparison argument in both variables proves minimality. Over C set u=x+iy and v=x−iy. Then x²+y²=uv and ∂ᵤ∂ᵥ=(1/4)(∂ₓ²+∂ᵧ²), so (1/4)Δf^(s+1)=(s+1)²f^s.","conclusion":"A polynomial automorphism preserves the defining differential-operator problem, so the nonmonomial quadratic has b(s)=(s+1)². Repeated roots carry actual multiplicity; they must not be discarded."}
limits: These are global polynomial examples in characteristic zero. General singularities may require local rather than global b-functions, elimination in a Weyl algebra, or additional singularity theory. The derivation does not establish that every proposed physical or statistical application admits a useful b-function.
extension: A worthwhile next calculation is to compute a local b-function for a chosen non-normal-crossing plane singularity, retaining the operator certificate and a separate minimality argument. An unverified candidate formula should be labeled as such.
